citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Motivation: extrinsic and intrinsic
items.core_explanation_md:
**Motivation** is the **drive within a person** that starts, guides and sustains behaviour.

**Extrinsic** motivation comes from **outside**: praise, trophies, money, recognition. **Intrinsic** motivation comes from **within**: the satisfaction of the task itself.

**Three components:** a **choice** to act, **perseverance** despite obstacles and **intensity** of effort. The courseware notes that rewards that are **expected** can **reduce** intrinsic motivation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A student who studies hard for the satisfaction of learning shows intensity; one who coasts shows the choice without the intensity.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between extrinsic and intrinsic motivation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Extrinsic comes from outside rewards, intrinsic from satisfaction in the task itself.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Content theories: ERG, Herzberg and McClelland
items.core_explanation_md:
**ERG (Alderfer):** three needs, **existence** (physical and mental well-being), **relatedness** (relationships) and **growth** (fulfilment).

**Herzberg:** **hygiene factors** (policies, supervision, relationships, working conditions, pay, status) **prevent dissatisfaction** and, if missing, lower effort; **motivators** (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, promotion, growth) **inspire** best effort.

**McClelland:** learned needs for **power, affiliation and achievement**. High achievers take **calculated risks**, want **quick feedback** and find the **task itself** rewarding.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These are called content theories because they say what motivates; the process theories say how motivation works.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of Herzberg's two groups lowers effort when absent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Hygiene factors.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Process theories: equity, expectancy and self-determination
items.core_explanation_md:
**Porter and Lawler:** performance leads to **rewards**, and rewards lead to **satisfaction**; satisfaction is **not simply the cause** of performance.

**Adams (equity):** people compare their **input-outcome balance** with **co-workers'**; a perceived **inequity** pushes them to restore fairness.

**Vroom (expectancy):** **M = V x I x E**, that is **valence** (value of the reward), **instrumentality** (belief that results bring the reward) and **expectancy** (belief that effort brings results). If **any one is zero**, motivation is lacking.

**Deci and Ryan (self-determination):** people are driven by a wish to improve themselves and feel more motivated when they **control the outcome**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: For leaders, the expectancy theory implies offering rewards people value, setting goals within reach and honouring promised incentives.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is Vroom's formula multiplicative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because if any one of valence, instrumentality or expectancy is zero, the product, and so the motivation, is zero.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Communication: models and levels
items.core_explanation_md:
**Communication** is **conveying meaning** between people through a **shared set of symbols**.

**Models:** the **linear model** follows Lasswell's questions of who, says what, through which channel, to whom and with what effect; **Shannon and Weaver** set it out as **origin, transmission, channel, receiver and destination**. The **dynamic model** treats communication as always developing.

**Levels:** **extra-personal** (with non-human entities), **interpersonal**, **intrapersonal**, **organisational** (up, down and across, and outward) and **mass**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In organisations, good communication supports learning, teamwork, safety, innovation and better decisions, and brevity works well with the newer workforce.

self_check.prompt_text: List the five components in the Shannon and Weaver sequence.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Origin of the information, transmission, the channel, the receiver and the destination.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Supervision: roles, qualities and importance
items.core_explanation_md:
**Supervision** means **overseeing** others and guiding their work to reach stated outputs.

**Two roles:** a **link** between management and workers (policies go down, complaints and suggestions go up) and a **guide, motivator and mentor**.

**Qualities:** **leadership**, **knowledge and skills**, **personal traits**, the right **degree of supervision** (too tight harms morale), **group cohesiveness** and **rapport with superiors**.

**Importance:** clear **orders**, **planning** the work, **proper assignment**, **better use of resources**, **motivation and discipline**, and a **two-way link** with management.

items.title: What controlling is and what it achieves
items.core_explanation_md:
**Controlling** is the **last function** of the management process. It checks whether work is going **as planned**, measures **how far actual performance differs** from predetermined benchmarks, finds the **causes** of the gap and **adjusts**.

**What it achieves:** it helps **reach goals**, **reduces errors**, makes **efficient use of resources**, **tests whether the standards were right**, builds **order and discipline**, improves **coordination**, **simplifies supervision and delegation**, and gives **feedback for the next plan**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because control compares results against standards, it can also show that a standard was set too high or too low.

self_check.prompt_text: State what the controlling function compares.
self_check.expected_takeaway: It compares actual performance with predetermined standards or benchmarks.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Limitations of control
items.core_explanation_md: **Limits to keep in mind:** control can be **costly**, especially for small firms; it is **hard to apply to non-quantitative standards** such as morale or team spirit; it gives **little control over external factors** (government policy, consumer behaviour, technology, competition); staff may **resist** it as a curb on freedom; **over-reliance** on controls can make supervision lax; **rigid rules slow work**; and **wrong controls** can expose the organisation to more errors and fraud.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These limits show why control must suit the organisation and the activity, not just be applied by habit.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is it hard to control morale?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because morale cannot be measured in quantitative terms against a standard.

items.title: Three types of control by timing
items.core_explanation_md:
| Type | When it acts | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Feedback control** | After the activity | Helps only **similar future** activity |
| **Concurrent control** | While the activity is carried out | **Immediate**, during the activity |
| **Proactive control** | Before problems arise | **Anticipates** and prevents problems |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A month-end review of last month's variances is feedback control; a supervisor correcting a process on the shop floor is concurrent control; a forecast-based warning before a shortage is proactive control.

self_check.prompt_text: Which control type can only improve similar future activity?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Feedback control.

items.title: The four steps of the control process and its link to planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** 1. **Set goals and standards**, clearly communicated (tangible, such as a Rs 100 crore sales target, or intangible). 2. **Compare actual performance** with them; measure results and gather feedback. 3. **Take corrective action promptly** where there are gaps. 4. **Keep monitoring** the effects of the corrective action until the problem is solved.

**Link to planning:** planning is the **foundation and originator** of control; control **returns information** for later planning; planning comes first and control is the **last step**; both look at the **future**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Planning without control cannot show whether plans are being carried out; control without planning has no standards to compare against.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can control not exist without planning?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because planning sets the objectives and standards against which performance is measured.

items.title: Break-even point
items.core_explanation_md:
The **break-even point** is the output at which **total revenue equals total cost**, so there is **neither profit nor loss**.

**In units = fixed cost / (selling price per unit - variable cost per unit)**. The denominator is the **contribution margin per unit**. The **margin of safety** is the part of actual sales **above** the break-even level.

assumptions: Constant price and variable cost per unit
Fixed costs stay fixed over the range
common_errors: Using total cost instead of fixed cost in the numerator
Using price minus total cost per unit in the denominator

items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware names break-even point, angle of incidence, contribution margin and margin of safety as the measures used; only the first, third and fourth are defined here.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the denominator of the break-even formula?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The contribution margin per unit, that is price less variable cost per unit.

items.title: Traditional techniques: observation, statistical reports and budgets
items.core_explanation_md:
**Personal observation:** the manager watches work **on the spot**, getting **first-hand information** and correcting at once; it is **time-consuming**.

**Statistical reports:** averages, percentages, ratios and the coefficient of determination, presented as **charts, graphs and tables**, show **areas needing attention**.

**Budgetary control:** plan the budget, **compare actual performance with it** and **act on deviations**. Typical budgets: **cash, sales, production, capital and material**. A risk is that the final budget proves **inaccurate and costly**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Subdividing company goals into departmental budgets makes day-to-day control easier.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two budgets organisations commonly prepare.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example the cash budget and the sales budget.

items.title: Return on investment (Du Pont form)
items.core_explanation_md:
**ROI = (net income / sales) x (sales / total investment)**, the **profit margin** times the **investment turnover**.

ROI rises if **sales grow proportionately more than investment**, or if **investment falls while sales are kept**.

assumptions: Net income, sales and investment are measured over the same period
common_errors: Using profit before tax in one factor and net income in another
Forgetting that sales cancel when the two factors are multiplied

items.expanded_explanation_md: Because sales cancel, ROI equals net income divided by total investment; the two-factor form shows whether margin or turnover is the lever.

self_check.prompt_text: What two ratios multiply to give ROI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Net income over sales and sales over total investment.

items.title: Ratios, responsibility centres, PERT and CPM, MIS and management audit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Ratio analysis:** **profitability, liquidity, solvency and turnover** ratios from the financial statements.

**Responsibility accounting:** four centres, **revenue, cost, profit and investment**.

**PERT** shows project activities in **sequence and timing**; **CPM** finds the **tasks needed for completion** and scheduling flexibility; the **critical path** is the **longest** sequence of activities that must finish on time.

**MIS** has two parts, **collection of data** and **management of data**. A **management audit** examines how the company uses its resources, is started by **top management**, may be done every **two or three years** and is **not compulsory**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Selecting among these techniques depends on the type of business, the users and the challenges faced, as well as cost, personnel and the dependability of the findings.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four responsibility centres.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Revenue, cost, profit and investment centres.

items.title: IT controls
items.core_explanation_md:
IT controls protect the **confidentiality, integrity and availability** of data and the sound running of the IT function.

**Techniques:** **organisational** (clear responsibilities), **management** (expert committees), **financial** (authorisation, **dual control**, **segregation of duties**, input and output checks), **data processing environment**, **physical access**, **logical access**, **SDLC** and **business continuity** controls.

**IT general controls** cover the IT environment, change management, access, incident handling, backup and recovery. **Application controls** work inside a programme: **completeness, validity, identification, authentication, authorisation and input** controls.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The CIO or CISO is accountable for the safety, accuracy and dependability of the systems that manage and report the company's data.

self_check.prompt_text: What do application controls check that general controls do not?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They check data inside a particular programme from input through processing to output.

items.title: COBIT and COSO
items.core_explanation_md:
**COBIT** is a framework of best practice for **governing and managing information and technology**. Its four domains are **planning and organising, acquiring and implementing, delivering and supporting, and monitoring and evaluating**.

**COSO** names five components of internal control: **control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: COBIT is the IT governance framework; COSO is the general internal control framework.

self_check.prompt_text: List the five COSO components.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring.

items.title: Why businesses need finance and how strategy is chosen
items.core_explanation_md:
**Long-term finance** sets up the project: it comes from **promoters' own equity** and, when the project is large, from **long-term borrowing**. **Bridge finance** is a **temporary loan** to cover the gap until long-term loans are released. The **debt equity ratio** says how the two share the burden; the general safe norm in the courseware is **Rs 100 of equity to Rs 200 of debt**.

**Working capital finance** funds the **gap between current assets and current liabilities**, and the bank expects the borrower to bring in its own contribution.

**Financial strategy** means choosing the **mix of sources** that gives the lowest cost and most advantage. **Clean (unsecured) finance** such as equity is the **costliest** because the lender has no assets to rely on.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The rate a company pays depends on its balance sheet, performance, track record of repayment and credit rating.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is clean finance costly?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the lender has no assets to fall back on, so it charges for the risk.

items.title: Equity capital: features, terms and trade-offs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Equity shares** are equal-value units; holders get **dividends**, a claim on **surplus assets on liquidation** and **voting rights**.

**Capital terms in order:** **authorised** (the maximum permitted), **issued**, **subscribed**, **called-up** and **paid-up** capital. **Calls in arrears** are called amounts not paid; **forfeited shares** are those cancelled for non-payment.

**For:** no compulsory dividend, no repayment, **risk capital**, ownership, lender comfort. **Against:** **highest cost of capital** (holders expect more for the risk), **costly to raise**, dividend is **paid from post-tax profit** (interest on loans is tax deductible) and wider ownership **dilutes control**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Equity gives lenders safety because a higher equity share cushions their loans.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is equity costlier than a loan even though no dividend is compulsory?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Holders expect higher returns for the higher risk, and dividends are paid from post-tax profit with no tax relief.

items.title: Internal accruals: retained profit and non-cash charges
items.core_explanation_md:
**Internal accruals** come from **retained profit after tax** plus **non-cash charges** such as depreciation and provisions.

**Advantages:** **no restriction** on use, **no servicing cost**, **readily available**, and **no dilution** of ownership.

**Drawbacks:** the **real cost is higher** because retained profit is **undeclared dividend**; shareholders (especially minority holders) lose **dividends**; the company cannot build a **dividend track record**; and money may go into **less scrutinised** projects. **Depreciation** adds cash but is **not a reserve** to pay dividends or issue bonus shares.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Retained earnings can become equity when converted into bonus shares, where regulations permit.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is retained profit not free?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It belongs to equity shareholders, who expect a return on it, so it carries an opportunity cost.

items.title: Preference shares: a quasi-risk capital
items.core_explanation_md:
**Preference shares** rank **ahead of equity** for dividend and for repayment on liquidation, but **behind secured debt**. The **dividend is fixed**, **not compulsory** unless the shares are **cumulative**, and paid from **post-tax profit** (not tax deductible).

Under the courseware's account of the Companies Act 2013 they must be **redeemable within 20 years** (infrastructure companies can exceed this). Holders have **limited voting rights**, but if dividend is unpaid for **two years or more** they can **vote on all resolutions**.

**Why raise it:** long-term funds, **no dilution of control**, a **known fixed cost** and it counts in **net worth**. **Drawbacks:** non-deductible dividend, redemption reserves cut retained earnings, and contingent voting rights create uncertainty.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The cumulative feature means unpaid dividends accumulate and are paid in a later year when profits allow.

self_check.prompt_text: When do preference shareholders get full voting rights?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When dividend has not been paid for two years or more.

items.title: Term loans: terms, security and covenants
items.core_explanation_md:
A **term loan** finances **long-lived tangible assets** and is repaid over a set period: **short term** is within a year, **medium** is 1 to 5 years and **long** is 5 to 10 years (housing 5 to 30).

**Interest** is fixed in advance and falls as principal is repaid. **Repayment** may be by instalments, EMI or a **bullet**, with a **moratorium** (grace period) on principal. **Foreign currency loans** carry **exchange risk**, which a **forward contract** can hedge. **Security** is a **charge on the assets financed**, sometimes with promoters' personal assets. A **WCTL** is a **short-term loan against current assets** for temporary liquidity strain. A **conversion clause** lets the loan turn into **equity** at an agreed price.

**Covenants** include a **board seat**, consent for mergers or expansion, **dividend limits**, **ratio maintenance**, borrowing ceilings and negative pledge.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Lenders use covenants to protect their interest, which can also improve the borrower's governance.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a moratorium on a term loan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A grace period during which principal repayment does not start, usually until the project earns cash.

items.title: Term loan trade-offs
items.core_explanation_md:
**For the borrower:** **control and shareholding are kept**, **interest is tax deductible**, long repayment is **cheaper in real terms** when inflation erodes the rupee, repayment can be **matched to cash flow**, and lenders are usually **considerate in difficulty**.

**Against:** **restrictive clauses** can hinder a dynamic firm, **heavy borrowing** lowers the rating, **too much debt** can become a **debt trap**, and **interest is a fixed cost**, so profits fall faster than sales when volume drops.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a low-inflation period the real rate of interest can turn out higher than expected.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does fixed interest hurt when volumes fall?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest does not fall with volume, so profits fall disproportionately.

items.title: Debentures: features and types
items.core_explanation_md:
A **debenture** is an instrument of a company evidencing a **debt**. **Features:** a promise to repay a **fixed amount on a fixed date**; **fixed interest** (**zero-coupon** bonds are issued at a **discount**); **no voting rights**; a **trustee** is needed if issued to **more than 500** persons; **convertible** debentures give equity and votes after conversion; a **call option** lets the **issuer** repay early, a **put option** lets the **investor** demand early redemption.

**Types:** by **tenure**, **security** (first or second charge), **convertibility** and **negotiability** (registered or the rare **bearer** debentures).

**Pros:** low cost, known interest and redemption date, **no dilution**. **Cons:** terms cannot be renegotiated, a **rating** may be needed, and a **redemption reserve** must be created.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Moving from equity to debentures lowers the cost of funds; dilution of control arises only when debentures convert.

self_check.prompt_text: Who holds the call option and who holds the put option on a debenture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The issuer holds the call option and the investor holds the put option.

items.title: Alternative finance and private equity stages
items.core_explanation_md:
**Alternatives outside banks and NBFCs:** **crowd funding, peer to peer lending, angel investors, venture capital, AIFs, mutual funds, REITs, InvITs** and **bootstrapping**.

**Private equity** is **patient** equity capital in **unlisted** high-growth companies, less liquid than listed stock.

**Stages:** **seed** (an idea), **start-up** (product development), **first stage** (commercialisation), **second stage** (working capital), **third stage** (expansion) and **bridge** (last round before a public offering).

**PIPE:** a private investment in a **listed** company's shares. **LBO:** purchase by a small group, **largely with debt**; **MBO:** an LBO in which **existing management** joins the buyers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Private equity investors seek long-term capital gains rather than regular reimbursement.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between an LBO and an MBO?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In an MBO the incumbent management is part of the buying group.

items.title: After-tax cost of interest versus dividend
items.core_explanation_md:
**Interest** on a loan is **tax deductible**, so its after-tax cost is **interest rate x (1 - tax rate)**.

**Dividend** is paid from **post-tax profit** and **not deductible**, so a dividend of the same percentage costs the **full percentage**.

Therefore, at the same headline rate, **debt is cheaper than preference or equity** after tax.

assumptions: Interest is fully deductible
The company has taxable profit
common_errors: Applying the tax saving to dividends
Using the tax rate as a percentage without converting

items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware stresses that the real cost of equity is higher because dividends get no tax relief.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a 10 per cent loan cost less than 10 per cent preference dividend?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest is tax deductible while preference dividend is not.

items.title: Financial leverage: borrowing to lift earnings per share
items.core_explanation_md:
**Financial leverage** means using **borrowed funds** to raise **EPS** without raising more equity. It pays only if the **assets bought with the debt earn more than the debt costs**.

It is **limited** because as **debt rises** lenders charge **more** or refuse, and the extra surplus may drop **below** the cost of borrowing, so EPS can **fall**. It is a **double-edged sword**.

**Measures:** **debt to assets**, **debt to equity**, **debt to EBITDA**, the **equity multiplier** (total assets over total equity) and **interest coverage** (EBIT over interest).
items.expanded_explanation_md: There is no single standard measure; each shows leverage from a different angle.

self_check.prompt_text: When does financial leverage raise EPS?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When the assets bought with borrowed money earn more than the cost of the borrowing.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Degree of financial leverage
items.core_explanation_md:
**DFL = % change in EPS / % change in EBIT**, which simplifies to **EBIT / EBT** because interest is a **fixed amount**.

**Reading it:** DFL **above 1** means a **given % change in EBIT produces a larger % change in EPS**. With **no interest**, DFL is **1**. At **break-even** (EBIT equals interest) EBT is nil and DFL is **undefined**; **below** it DFL is **negative**.

assumptions: Interest is a fixed amount
Tax rate and number of shares are constant
No preference dividend
common_errors: Using EBT over EBIT
Treating a company below break-even as having a meaningful positive DFL

items.expanded_explanation_md: A DFL of 1.5 means a 10 per cent rise in EBIT lifts EPS by about 15 per cent, and a 10 per cent fall cuts it by about 15 per cent.

self_check.prompt_text: What is DFL when a firm has no interest burden?
self_check.expected_takeaway: One, because EBT equals EBIT.

citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Degree of operating leverage
items.core_explanation_md:
**Operating leverage** comes from **fixed operating costs** (other than interest).

**DOL = % change in EBIT / % change in sales = contribution / EBIT**, where **contribution = sales less variable cost** and **EBIT = contribution less fixed cost**.

With **no fixed cost**, DOL is **1**. The **higher the fixed cost**, the **higher the DOL**, and DOL **falls** as sales move **further above break-even**. At **EBIT of nil** DOL is **undefined**.

assumptions: Fixed cost and price and variable cost per unit are constant over the range
common_errors: Using sales instead of contribution in the numerator
Using EBT in the denominator

items.expanded_explanation_md: A firm with high fixed costs and low variable costs gains sharply when sales rise and loses sharply when they fall.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to DOL as sales rise further above break-even?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It falls towards 1.

items.core_explanation_md:

| **High leverage** | High | **Higher** | **Higher** |

self_check.expected_takeaway: Because more contribution is needed before fixed cost is covered.

items.title: Combined (total) leverage
items.core_explanation_md:
**DTL = DOL x DFL = contribution / EBT.**

It measures how a **% change in sales** is magnified into a **% change in EBT or EPS** by **both** the fixed operating costs and the fixed financial costs together.

For example, a DTL of **6** means a **10 per cent** change in sales changes EBT by about **60 per cent**.

assumptions: Fixed operating cost and fixed interest
No preference dividend
common_errors: Adding DOL and DFL instead of multiplying
Using EBIT in place of EBT in the denominator

items.expanded_explanation_md: EBIT cancels in the product, which is why contribution over EBT gives the combined leverage directly.

self_check.prompt_text: How is DTL related to DOL and DFL?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is their product.

items.title: Why firms make capital investment decisions
items.core_explanation_md:
The goal is to **maximise shareholders' wealth**. A firm that **never invests**, not even to replace worn plant, **shrinks**. One that **skips good opportunities** loses wealth. One that **invests in every project returning more than shareholders could earn elsewhere** **increases wealth**.

The decision first asks **how much is needed**, then the **source, cost, form and timing** of funds.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware contrasts three companies with identical opportunities but different investment policies.

self_check.prompt_text: Which investments increase owners' wealth?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Those whose return exceeds what the shareholders could have earned themselves.

items.title: Estimating project cash flows
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three elements:** **initial** (capital expenditure and net working capital), **operating** (yearly inflows and outflows) and **terminal** (what remains at the end of life).

**Four principles:** **separation** (keep financing flows such as interest out of the investment flows), **incremental** (count only costs that arise **because of** the project), **post-tax** (use **after-tax** flows) and **consistency** (a discount rate consistent with the flows).

**CFAT:** sales less variable cost, less fixed cash cost and depreciation = **EBT**; less tax = **EAT**; **add back depreciation** = **cash inflow after tax**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Depreciation is deducted to find tax but added back because it is not a cash outflow.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is depreciation added back to earnings after tax?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because it is a non-cash charge; it only reduces tax.

items.title: Project cost and what to test in it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Project cost** includes **fixed assets** (land, building, plant, power lines, environment equipment, intangible assets), **installation**, **direct costs of setting up** and other **pre-operative costs**, capitalised to the assets.

**Tests applied:** **necessity**, **best combination**, **competitive bargaining**, **recoverable duties** (input tax credit is **not** part of cost where recoverable), **buy or lease**, **asset life**, **justification**, **environmental impact**, **growth** and **sustainability**, and the **projected returns**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A very long life means high repair cost and old technology; a very short life means frequent replacement.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is recoverable input tax credit excluded from asset cost?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the tax is offset against duties collected, so it is not a real cost.

items.title: Payback period
items.core_explanation_md:
**Payback period = investment / annual net cash inflow** when inflows are **equal**.

When inflows **differ**, add **cumulative** inflows year by year until they equal the investment; the part of the last year is **balance still to recover / that year's inflow**.

**Cash inflow = profit after tax + depreciation.**

Payback is **simple** and shows **risk** (shorter is safer), but it **ignores the time value of money** and **all flows after payback**. The **discounted payback** uses **present values**.

assumptions: Equal annual cash inflows
Inflow accrues evenly in the final year
common_errors: Using profit instead of cash inflow
Forgetting the fraction of the final year

items.expanded_explanation_md: With unequal flows, a payback of 3.25 years means the first three years recover all but the last quarter of the fourth year.

self_check.prompt_text: What does payback ignore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The time value of money and all cash flows after the payback period.

items.title: Accounting rate of return
items.core_explanation_md:
**ARR = average annual profit after tax and depreciation / investment x 100.**

**Two bases for investment:** the **initial investment**, or the **average investment = half of (initial investment - salvage value) + salvage value**.

ARR uses **accounting profit** (not cash flow) and **ignores the time value of money**, so two projects with the **same ARR** but different timing of benefits look alike.

assumptions: Straight line depreciation

common_errors: Using cash inflow instead of profit

items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware notes an internal inconsistency: the numerator belongs to owners while the denominator is total investment.

self_check.prompt_text: How is average investment found?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Half of (initial investment less salvage value) plus salvage value.

items.title: Net present value
items.core_explanation_md:
**NPV = present value of net cash inflows - initial investment**, discounting each year's flow at the **required rate**.

**Decision:** **accept if NPV is positive**; **zero** means the project neither adds nor loses value; **negative** means reject. Among **mutually exclusive** projects, take the **higher NPV**.

**Working capital:** an **increase** is an **outflow**, a **decrease** an **inflow**. **EAC** compares assets with **different lives**.

variables.name: Net cash inflow in year t
Required rate of return (cost of capital)

assumptions: Cash flows occur at year ends
The discount rate is known and constant
common_errors: Discounting the initial investment
Using an inconsistent discount rate

items.expanded_explanation_md: NPV is the amount by which the value of the business rises if the project is undertaken.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a zero NPV mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The project earns exactly the required rate, adding neither value nor loss.

items.title: IRR and MIRR
items.core_explanation_md:
**IRR** is the discount rate at which **NPV = 0**. Find it by **trial and error**, then **interpolate**: lower rate + (NPV at lower rate / (NPV at lower + absolute NPV at higher)) x the gap between the rates. **Accept if IRR exceeds the cost of capital.**

**Limits:** **multiple IRRs** with **alternating cash flows**, and the assumption that inflows are **reinvested at the IRR**.

**MIRR** fixes this: **PVC** = present value of costs at the cost of capital; **TV** = inflows compounded to the end at the cost of capital; **MIRR solves PVC = TV / (1 + MIRR)^n**, giving **one** answer.

Present value of costs at the cost of capital
Number of periods to the end of the project

assumptions: Inflows are reinvested at the cost of capital
Costs are financed at the cost of capital
common_errors: Compounding inflows at the IRR instead of the cost of capital
Using the number of cash flows instead of the number of periods

items.expanded_explanation_md: Both IRR and MIRR can mislead when ranking projects of different sizes, because a larger project with a lower rate can have the higher NPV.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can IRR give multiple answers?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When cash flows change sign more than once, the NPV equation can have several roots.

items.title: Profitability index and capital rationing
items.core_explanation_md:
**PI = sum of discounted cash inflows / initial cash outlay.**

**PI above 1** means profitable; **below 1** unprofitable. A **higher PI** ranks higher, even where another project has **larger absolute inflows**, because PI is **per rupee invested**.

**Capital rationing** limits the funds available; firms respond with norms such as a **higher IRR or PI hurdle**.

assumptions: Same discount rate for all projects
common_errors: Using NPV instead of present value of inflows in the numerator

items.expanded_explanation_md: PI above 1 is equivalent to a positive NPV for a given project.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a project with the largest inflows have a low PI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because its outlay is also very large, so inflow per rupee invested is low.

items.title: Social cost benefit analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
**SCBA** is used by **governments and local bodies** for **infrastructure** such as airports, ports and dams.

It gives **negative** value to **social costs** (pollution, loss of mangroves, health hazards) and **positive** value to **social benefits** (time and fuel savings, employment, better living standards).

The project is **beneficial** if the **net social result is positive** and at least equal to the project cost.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Unlike private appraisal, it counts costs and benefits to society, not only cash flows to the owner.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two social costs and two social benefits.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Costs: pollution and loss of mangroves. Benefits: time savings and employment.

items.title: What is different about foreign investment
items.core_explanation_md:
**Differences:** work culture, **legal and currency systems**, accounting standards, trade barriers and language.

**Cash flows** are in the **foreign currency**, so **exchange rate volatility** matters, especially over a long project. The currency used for analysis should be the one that **dominates** the project.

The **spot rate** applies to a **current** deal and the **forward rate** to a **future** one, adjusted for the **interest rate difference** and the **time**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Elaborate workings and several exchange rate scenarios may be needed for a long project.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The forward rate.

items.title: International portfolio investment and its channels
items.core_explanation_md:
**IPI** is investment in **foreign securities** (treasury bills, mutual funds, listed equities, debt) through **designated remittance channels**, in the **local currency** of the country invested in.

**Benefits:** **diversification** and a **better risk-return trade-off**. **Barriers:** political or economic uncertainty, **price controls** and language. **Asset allocation** and **hedging** (for example a forward contract) manage risk.

**Direct channels:** **ADRs, GDRs** and **FDI**. **Indirect channels:** intermediaries such as **mutual funds and ETFs**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Developed markets offer variety and stable exchange rates, which lower risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Name one direct and one indirect channel for foreign portfolio investment.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Direct: ADRs or GDRs. Indirect: mutual funds or ETFs.

items.title: Exchange risk, country risk and the return on foreign investment
items.core_explanation_md:
**Exchange risk:** the **home-currency value** of the investment falls because the **local currency depreciates** or the **home currency strengthens**.

**Country risk:** **political developments, restrictions, legal system, turbulence and change of government**.

**Return:** **more liquid** assets give a **lower return**, **secured** assets give less than **unsecured**; a country with a **stable exchange rate** gives better returns, and **reinvesting dividends** raises them.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Foreign investment carries exchange and country risk on top of the usual risks.

self_check.prompt_text: Give two examples of country risk.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Political upheaval and restrictions on free trade or capital movement.

items.title: CAPM and APT expected return
items.core_explanation_md:
**CAPM:** **re = rf + beta x (rm - rf)**. Beta measures **systematic risk** against the market; **rm - rf** is the **market risk premium**.

**APT:** the expected return is the **risk-free rate plus, for each macroeconomic factor, beta x risk premium**. It uses **several factors** (GDP, inflation, gold, stock index), not just the market.

variables.name: Sensitivity of the security to the market

assumptions: A single market factor drives systematic risk
common_errors: Applying beta to the market return instead of the premium
Adding the risk-free rate twice

items.expanded_explanation_md: Beta is the covariance of the security's return with the market return divided by the variance of the market return.

self_check.prompt_text: How does APT differ from CAPM?
self_check.expected_takeaway: APT uses several macroeconomic factors with their own betas and premiums; CAPM uses only the market.

items.title: Risk-adjusted discount rate and expected spot rate
items.core_explanation_md:
**Foreign risk-adjusted rate:** first find the **risk premium** the company wants at home, **(1 + rp) = (1 + home required rate) / (1 + home risk-free rate)**; then **(1 + r_a) = (1 + foreign risk-free rate) x (1 + rp)**.

**Expected spot rate (interest rate parity):** **S_t = S_0 x [(1 + home risk-free) / (1 + foreign risk-free)]^t**. The currency of the **higher interest rate** is expected to **depreciate**.

variables.name: Expected spot rate at time t (home currency per unit of foreign)

assumptions: Interest rate parity holds
Rates are annual and constant
common_errors: Inverting the ratio of interest rates
Using simple instead of compound growth over several years

items.expanded_explanation_md: With a higher home interest rate the foreign currency is expected to be dearer in rupees in later years.

self_check.prompt_text: If home interest rates exceed foreign rates, what is expected of the exchange rate (home per foreign)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is expected to rise, so the home currency depreciates.

items.title: Home currency and foreign currency approaches
items.core_explanation_md:
| Step | Home currency approach | Foreign currency approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Forecast **spot rates** for each year | Find the **foreign risk-adjusted rate** |
| 2 | **Convert** inflows to **rupees** | **Discount** inflows in the **foreign currency** |
| 3 | **Discount** at the **home risk-adjusted rate** | **Convert** the present value at the **current spot rate** |
| 4 | Subtract the investment (at current spot) | Subtract the investment (at current spot) |

With **consistent** inputs the two give the **same NPV**; small differences come from **rounding**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Payback, IRR and the profitability index are applied the same way once the cash flows are in one currency.

self_check.prompt_text: Which approach converts each year's inflow at a different spot rate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The home currency approach.

items.title: Transfer pricing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Transfer prices** are charged between **related parties in different countries**. They can be set to **shift profit to a tax haven**, so the **OECD** recommends **transfer pricing rules** for related party transactions, now in many countries' tax laws.

Breaches attract **financial burdens** that can be **prohibitive**, so **international investments** must be studied with these rules in mind.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The principle is that related parties should price transactions as unrelated parties would.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do countries impose transfer pricing rules?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To stop related parties manipulating prices to move profits to low-tax jurisdictions.

items.title: Sources of risk in a project
items.core_explanation_md:
Capital budgeting looks **years ahead**, so cost and revenue estimates are **uncertain**.

**Kinds of risk:** **project-specific** (high technology, an unstable country, hazardous or polluting processes), **competitive** (rivals enter when demand rises), **market** (seasonal or policy-dependent business, scaling up to national or international markets), **exchange risk** abroad and **corporate events**. All of them can hit **sales, cost and profitability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A plant that pollutes may face closure orders and must spend on pollution control even before scrutiny arrives.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two project-specific risks.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example reliance on high technology and use of hazardous chemicals.

citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Sensitivity analysis: one variable at a time
items.core_explanation_md:
**Sensitivity analysis** changes **one variable at a time** (investment, sales, variable cost, fixed cost, cost of capital) while the rest stay at expected values, and records the effect on **NPV or IRR**.

**Steps:** identify the factors that drive NPV; understand how they link; measure the **% change in NPV** for the same % adverse change in each. The variable with the **largest % change** is the one the project is **most sensitive** to.

**Limits:** only **one variable at a time**, shows **only NPV**, and ranges are **subjective**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: It shows how robust or weak the project is and where to tighten the plan.

self_check.prompt_text: How do you find the variable a project is most sensitive to?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Apply the same adverse percentage change to each variable and pick the one causing the largest percentage change in NPV.

citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Scenario analysis: all variables together
items.core_explanation_md:
**Scenario analysis** moves **all variables together** in three cases: **pessimistic** (worst values), **expected** and **optimistic** (best values).

It goes beyond sensitivity analysis, but it is not certain that **all variables move the same way at once**.

You can also **mix** cases, such as certain cash flows in the early years and a worst case in the last year, and recompute NPV.
items.expanded_explanation_md: With probabilities attached to the scenarios, an expected NPV can be calculated.

self_check.prompt_text: How does scenario analysis differ from sensitivity analysis?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It changes all the variables together rather than one at a time.

items.title: Hillier model: standard deviation of NPV
items.core_explanation_md:
The **risk** of a project is the **dispersion of its cash flows**, measured by the **standard deviation of NPV**, with the **risk-free rate** as the discount rate.

**Perfectly correlated** flows: **sigma(NPV) = sum of sigma_t / (1 + i)^t**.

**Uncorrelated** flows: **sigma(NPV) = square root of the sum of sigma_t squared / (1 + i)^(2t)**.

The **uncorrelated** case gives the **smaller** figure, because variations offset.

variables.name: Standard deviation of the cash flow in year t

assumptions: Cash flows in different years are independent (uncorrelated case)
Discounting is at the risk-free rate
common_errors: Adding variances without discounting
Using the perfectly correlated formula for independent flows

items.expanded_explanation_md: A lower deviation of cash flows from their mean means a lower risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Which case gives the larger standard deviation of NPV?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The case of perfectly correlated cash flows.

items.title: Simulation analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
**Simulation** builds an artificial version of the project and runs it **many times**.

**Steps:** prepare the model; calculate NPV; separate **parameters** (set by the decision maker) from **exogenous variables** (outside the model, such as rainfall); estimate **probability distributions** of the exogenous variables; **draw random values**; compute NPV for each draw; **repeat**; **plot the distribution of NPV**.

It is done by **computer**, handles **many variables**, but **needs judgement** and gives **misleading results** if **correlations** between variables are mishandled.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The result is a frequency distribution of NPV showing how likely different outcomes are.

self_check.prompt_text: What is an exogenous variable?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A variable whose value is determined outside the model and cannot be controlled by the decision maker.

items.title: Decision tree and expected value
items.core_explanation_md:
A **decision tree** has **branches** (decisions) and **nodes** (outcomes with their **probabilities**).

**Draw** the tree, then **evaluate backwards** from the last branch: at each node **expected value = sum of (reward x probability)**; keep the **higher expected value** and **discard the other**.

Example: NPV of Rs 5 lakh with probability 0.4 and Rs 4 lakh with probability 0.6 gives **5 x 0.4 + 4 x 0.6 = Rs 4.4 lakh**.

assumptions: Probabilities of the branches from a node add up to one
common_errors: Adding rewards without weighting by probability
Evaluating from the first branch instead of the last

items.expanded_explanation_md: As more uncertainties are added the tree grows, so the manager decides which factors to include.

self_check.prompt_text: In which direction is a decision tree evaluated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Backwards, from the last branch to the starting point.

items.title: Corporate risk analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
A **new project changes the firm's overall risk profile**, just as a new security changes the risk of a portfolio. A project that looks risky **alone** may be a **complement** to the firm's other projects.

**Diversification** or **backward integration** must be judged **for the whole firm**. It can **reduce overall risk** and cushion a **cyclical downturn**, but **shareholders can diversify themselves** and the firm's **identity** should not be lost.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The stand-alone view and the corporate view of a project may therefore give different answers.

self_check.prompt_text: Why might a risky project still suit the firm?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because it can complement the firm's other projects and lower the combined risk.

items.title: Managing risk: the toolkit
items.core_explanation_md:
Some risks can be **eliminated** by changing method; others only **mitigated**.

**Tools:** **cost control** (outsource or lease fixed assets), prudent **financial leverage**, calculating **break-even** before **pricing**, **sequential investment** (a decision tree helps), **information intelligence** (take expert advice first), **strategic alliances**, **insurance**, **supply chain** relationships, **derivatives** (options give a **right** for a **premium**; **call** = right to buy, **put** = right to sell; risky if mismanaged), **shorter time to market** and **contingency planning**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware stresses never testing the depth of the water with both feet.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a put option give the holder?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The right to sell the underlying at a predetermined price on or before a given date.

items.title: Risk-adjusted discount rate
items.core_explanation_md:
When a project is riskier than the firm's normal business, **raise the discount rate**: **r_k = i + n + d_k**, where **i** is the **risk-free rate**, **n** the adjustment for the firm's **normal risk** and **d_k** the **differential risk** of project k (positive or negative).

A firm may use a **low** rate for **replacement**, a **moderate** one for **expansion** and a **high** one for **new ventures**. Accept the project only if **NPV is positive at the RADR**.

**Drawbacks:** **d_k is hard to estimate**, and the method assumes risk rises at a **constant rate** with time.

variables.name: Risk-adjusted discount rate for project k
Adjustment for the firm's normal risk
Adjustment for the project's differential risk

assumptions: Risk premiums are additive
Risk is assumed to grow at a constant rate over time
common_errors: Discounting at the risk-free rate only
Applying the same premium to every kind of project

items.expanded_explanation_md: The differential risk is positive if the project is riskier than the firm's existing business and negative if it is safer.

self_check.prompt_text: What is d_k?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The adjustment for the project's differential risk compared with the firm's existing risk profile.

items.title: Certainty equivalent method
items.core_explanation_md:
The **certainty equivalent coefficient** = **certain amount acceptable / expected risky amount**. A **higher risk** gives a **lower** coefficient.

**NPV = sum of (coefficient x expected after-tax cash flow) / (1 + risk-free rate)^t, less initial investment.**

It is **conceptually better** than the RADR because it does **not** assume risk rises at a constant rate, but it is **harder to apply** because each year needs its own coefficient.

variables.name: Certainty equivalent coefficient in year t
Expected after-tax cash flow in year t

assumptions: Discounting is at the risk-free rate because risk is already in the coefficients
common_errors: Discounting certainty equivalents at a risk-adjusted rate (double counting risk)
Using a coefficient above 1 for a risky flow

items.expanded_explanation_md: The example coefficient 11,000 / (10,000 x 0.6 + 15,000 x 0.4) = 0.92 says the investor would swap the risky prospect for 92 per cent of its expected value.

self_check.prompt_text: Which rate discounts certainty equivalent cash flows?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The risk-free rate.

items.title: Selecting projects under risk: judgement and payback
items.core_explanation_md:
**Judgemental evaluation:** senior management, a committee or the Board debates **pros, cons, risks and rewards**. It is **subjective** but usually the **first** step.

**How quickly the project becomes risk free:** treating risk as a **function of time**, a **shorter payback** gives more comfort. Critics say risk **evens out** over the long term, so payback should not be the only test.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Payback is used to control risk by bringing the recovery of funds closer.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a shorter payback period attractive under risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Uncertainty increases with time, so recovering the investment sooner reduces exposure.

items.title: Risk analysis in practice
items.core_explanation_md:
**Revenue:** estimate **conservatively**. **Cost:** add a **safety margin of 10 to 30 per cent** depending on the cost type, plus a **contingency**. Build in **flexibility** (a **cut-off point** beyond which funding stops) and fix the **payback** in advance.

Then run **sensitivity** and **scenario** analysis. In the courseware's survey-based order the methods used are sensitivity analysis, scenario analysis, the risk-adjusted discount rate and decision tree analysis.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware treats cost as a committed amount that needs margins for escalation, unlike revenue, which is not under the firm's control.

self_check.prompt_text: What safety margin does the courseware suggest for cost estimates?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Between 10 and 30 per cent, depending on the type of cost.

items.title: CVP analysis in decision making
items.core_explanation_md:
**Cost, volume and price** drive profit and the **break-even point**. **Fixed cost per unit falls** as volume rises; **price** affects profitability and decides the break-even; a **new product** has high cost and needs an **affordable price**, which **delays break-even**.

**CVP answers questions such as:** how profit changes if **price is cut and volume raised**; how much **extra volume** pays for **higher fixed cost**; whether staff should get **salary, commission or both**; and the effect of **swings in sales, price, output or cost**. **Uncontrollable events** (war, floods, pandemics, trade policy) must be allowed for.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the factors influence one another, a change in one calls for reworking the whole analysis.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a new product delay break-even?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Volumes are low and cost per unit high, and the price must be kept affordable to attract buyers.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Activity based CVP: break-even with set-up costs
items.core_explanation_md:
In **activity based CVP** a cost that traditional CVP lumps into fixed cost is separated by **cost driver**. For set-ups: **number of set-ups = units / batch size**.

**Break-even units = (fixed cost + number of set-ups x cost per set-up) / contribution per unit.**

**Larger batches** mean **fewer set-ups**, so lower set-up cost and a **lower break-even** (less any extra cost such as storage).

assumptions: Constant price and variable cost per unit
Set-up cost driven only by the number of batches
common_errors: Counting set-up cost twice
Forgetting extra storage cost when batches grow

items.expanded_explanation_md: In the courseware example, doubling the batch size halves the set-ups and lowers the break-even despite an added storage cost.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to the number of set-ups when batch size is doubled?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It halves.

items.title: Relevant, sunk and opportunity cost
items.core_explanation_md:
**Relevant costs** are **future costs that differ between alternatives**. **Irrelevant costs** are unaffected by the decision.

**Sunk costs** are **already incurred** (road tax on a car you own) and are **irrelevant**. **Avoidable** costs are relevant; **unavoidable** ones are not.

**Opportunity cost** is the **benefit lost** by choosing one option over another; it needs **no cash payment** and arises **only when resources are scarce** (a machine at 95 per cent capacity, not at 60 per cent).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Discarding irrelevant data simplifies the decision.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a sunk cost irrelevant?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because it has been incurred already and will be the same whichever alternative is chosen.

items.title: Applying relevant costs: make or buy, special orders, closing a unit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Make or buy:** compare the **avoidable** cost of making (materials, labour, variable overhead and **special tools**) with the **buying price**; add the value of **space released**.

**Special order:** accept if the **extra revenue exceeds the extra relevant cost**; check effects on **existing customers** and **credit terms**.

**Material in stock:** the relevant cost of units already held is the **price they would fetch if sold** (not the original cost); extra units cost the **current purchase price**.

**Close a unit:** compare its income with the expenses that **would be avoided**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Other relevant uses include dropping a product line, outsourcing and heavy discount offers.

self_check.prompt_text: Which price is relevant for stock that would otherwise be sold?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The price it would fetch if sold, not what was originally paid.

items.title: Activity based costing: cost driver rates
items.core_explanation_md:
**ABC** assigns costs by the **activities that cause them** rather than by volume alone.

**Terms:** **cost object** (product, service or customer), **cost pool** (costs of an activity), **cost driver** (what changes the activity's cost).

**Activity cost driver rate = total cost of the activity / total activity driver quantity.**

**Cost to a product = driver rate x quantity of the driver the product uses.**

variables.name: Total number of units of the cost driver
Cost per unit of the driver

assumptions: Costs in a pool vary with a single driver
common_errors: Dividing by units produced instead of driver quantity
Using the traditional labour hour rate for all overheads

items.expanded_explanation_md: ABC shows product and customer profitability and gives a clearer view of process efficiency than volume-based allocation.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a cost driver?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A factor that causes a change in the cost of an activity.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Steps in an ABC system
items.core_explanation_md:
1. Identify the **costing project**. 2. Identify the **activities**. 3. Find the **direct cost** of products. 4. Relate **overheads** to the activities. 5. Spread **support services** across primary activities. 6. Determine the **activity cost drivers**. 7. Compute the **total cost** of the products or objects.

**Traditional** costing allocates overheads on **volume** (units or labour hours); **ABC** allocates on **drivers** such as purchase orders and inspections.
items.expanded_explanation_md: ABC is approximately right rather than precisely wrong, which is why it supports pricing and outsourcing decisions.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two cost drivers.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example number of purchase orders and number of inspections.

items.title: Ethical and non-financial considerations
items.core_explanation_md:
Decisions are **not based on profit alone**. A pollution unit in a cement plant may be uneconomic yet approved for **environmental** reasons.

**Questions to ask:** is it **true**, a **breach of trust**, **respectful**, **responsible**, **fair**, **compassionate**, **civil**?

An **ethical framework** builds **trust, respect, responsibility, fairness, care and civic duty** across the organisation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Fairness means treating people with equality and without favouritism or discrimination.

self_check.prompt_text: Why might a firm approve an uneconomic pollution control unit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because environmental and social responsibility are non-financial considerations that also count.

citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Character-based decision making and supply chain responsibility
items.core_explanation_md:
**Pillars:** **trustworthiness, respect, responsibility, fairness, caring and citizenship**.

**Seven steps:** **stop and think, clarify goals, determine facts, develop options, consider consequences, choose, monitor and modify.**

The model warns against **rationalisations** such as **"everyone's doing it"**, **"it doesn't hurt anyone"** and **"if it's necessary, it's ethical"**, and rests on the **Golden Rule**: help when you can and avoid harm when you can.

A firm that **outsources** production is still **morally responsible** for supplier conduct, for example **child labour**. It can adopt a **code of conduct**, **audit suppliers**, **penalise breaches** and **disclose its suppliers**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Ignoring a problem in the supply chain can also harm the business through reputation.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the first step of the seven step path?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Stop and think.

items.title: Book value, market value and enterprise value
items.core_explanation_md:
**Book value** comes from the **balance sheet**. **Market value** comes from the market: **market capitalisation = number of shares x share price**, an **equity** value.

**Enterprise (firm) value** covers the **whole company**: **equity value + short-term debt + long-term debt + current portion of long-term debt + capital leases + preferred securities + non-controlling interests + other non-operating liabilities, less cash and cash equivalents.**

**Fair market value** is the price between a **willing buyer and a willing seller**, neither under compulsion and both **reasonably informed**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Management aims to maximise firm value, and mergers, ESOPs and regulatory pricing all need valuation.

self_check.prompt_text: What is deducted when moving from equity value plus debt to enterprise value?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cash and cash equivalents.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Market, income and cost approaches
items.core_explanation_md:
| Approach | Idea | Suits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Market** | Price of **recent transactions or comparable assets**, adjusted for size and quality | Where **comparables** exist |
| **Income** | **Present value of expected earnings or cash flows** | Going concerns with predictable cash flows |
| **Cost (asset-based)** | **Assets less liabilities**, cost to rebuild or replace | **Asset-intensive** firms and **holding companies** |

No one approach fits every case. Choose by **basis of value, advantages and disadvantages, appropriateness and data availability**; when more than one is used, **reconcile** the results rather than simply average them.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The four methods for a firm are adjusted book value, stock and debt, direct comparison and discounted cash flow.

self_check.prompt_text: Which approach suits a holding company?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The cost (asset-based) approach.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Adjusted book value: replacement cost and liquidation value
items.core_explanation_md:
**Two ways to get book value:** **investor claims** (share capital + reserves + loans) or **total assets less current liabilities and provisions**. Both agree.

**Why book may mislead:** **inflation** (historical cost), **obsolescence** and **organisational capital** is not on the balance sheet.

**Replacement cost:** **cash** at face value; **receivables** less a **provision**; **stocks** at current cost or sale price less costs; **land** at market value; **buildings** at cost less physical depreciation; **plant** at the price of comparable used assets plus **transport and installation**; **non-operating assets** at market value.

**Liquidation value:** what the assets would fetch **sold at once**; it ignores organisational capital and suits a firm **worth more dead than alive**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The adjusted book value approach suits businesses whose value lies mainly in tangible assets.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does liquidation value ignore organisational capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It values the firm as a collection of assets that can be sold separately, not as a going concern.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Stock and debt approach
items.core_explanation_md:
For a company whose securities are **listed**, value is the **current market value of all outstanding securities**: **market value of equity + market value of debt**.

It rests on **market efficiency**: the price reflects all available information. Some appraisers **average** recent prices to dampen volatility around the valuation date; if the market is **efficient**, **the price on the date should be used** and averaging reduces accuracy.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is the quickest method, but it depends entirely on how well the market prices the securities.

self_check.prompt_text: What assumption underlies the stock and debt approach?
self_check.expected_takeaway: That the market is efficient, so the traded price reflects intrinsic value.

items.title: Direct comparison with multiples
items.core_explanation_md:
The approach rests on the **principle of substitution**: a buyer will not pay more than the cost of a **comparable** with the same utility.

**Steps:** analyse the **economy**, the **industry** and the **company**; find **comparable companies**; **adjust their statements**; compute the multiple **v/x** (value to an observable variable) and check it is **stable**; apply it to the target.

**Common multiples:** **EV/sales, EV/EBIT, P/E, price to book, price to sales**. **PEG = P/E divided by expected growth rate** corrects for growth differences.

**Value = multiple x target's variable.**

variables.name: Peer multiple of value to an observable variable
Target's figure for the variable (for example EPS or EBIT)

assumptions: Comparable companies are truly similar
The multiple is stable across the peers
common_errors: Applying an enterprise value multiple and reading it as equity value
Using a listed company multiple unadjusted for an unlisted target

items.expanded_explanation_md: An EV multiple gives enterprise value, from which debt is deducted to get equity value.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the PEG ratio correct for?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Differences in expected growth between companies.

items.title: Direct comparison: real estate and the limits of multiples
items.core_explanation_md:
**Real estate:** find the property's **highest and best use**, find **comparable sales**, make **time adjustments first**, then **other adjustments**: **add** for features where the subject is **superior**, **subtract** where it is **inferior**.

**Advantages:** multiples are **easy to find** and reflect market pricing.

**Weaknesses:** multiples can be **manipulated**; the appraiser may **choose comparables to confirm a bias**; and multiples **carry the market's over or undervaluation**. Valuing an **unlisted** firm on a **listed** technology company's P/E may **overvalue** it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: No two firms are identical in risk and growth, so adjustments and judgement are always needed.

self_check.prompt_text: In what order should adjustments be made to a comparable sale?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Time adjustments first, then the other adjustments.

items.title: DCF valuation of a firm: explicit period plus terminal value
items.core_explanation_md:
**Value of the firm = PV of free cash flows in the explicit forecast period + PV of the terminal (continuing) value + value of non-operating assets.**

The **explicit period** is typically **5 to 15 years**, after which the firm is assumed to reach a **stable level**.

**Six steps:** 1. **analyse historical performance**; 2. **calculate free cash flow**; 3. **calculate WACC**; 4. **forecast free cash flows and discount at WACC**; 5. **find the terminal value and its present value**; 6. **add the parts and the non-operating assets**.

variables.name: Free cash flow in year t
Terminal value at the end of year T

assumptions: Cash flows at year ends
Non-operating assets are valued separately
common_errors: Discounting the terminal value only to year T-1
Counting non-operating income inside free cash flow

items.expanded_explanation_md: Because firms are assumed to last indefinitely, the terminal value captures flows after the explicit period.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a terminal value needed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the firm is expected to continue beyond the explicit forecast period.

items.title: NOPLAT, ROIC, net investment and free cash flow
items.core_explanation_md:
**NOPLAT = EBIT - taxes on EBIT**, where EBIT excludes **interest** and **non-operating income**, and the tax is what the firm would pay **with no debt**.

**ROIC = NOPLAT / operating invested capital** (opening or average, used **consistently**).

**Net investment = gross investment - depreciation = (net fixed assets + net current assets) at year end less the same at the start.**

**Free cash flow = NOPLAT - net investment** (or **NOPLAT + depreciation - gross investment**).

items.title: WACC and the continuing value
items.core_explanation_md:
**WACC = w_d x r_d + w_p x r_p + w_e x r_e**, using **after-tax** debt cost, **market value weights** and **nominal** terms.

**Continuing value by two methods:** **growing FCF perpetuity: PV_T = FCF(T+1) / (WACC - g)**; **value driver: PV_T = NOPLAT(T+1) x (1 - g/r) / (WACC - g)**, where **r** is the **return on new investment** and **g** the **constant growth after the explicit period**.

The two agree when FCF equals **NOPLAT x (1 - g/r)**.

items.title: The idea behind DCF valuation
items.core_explanation_md:
The value of any asset is the **sum of its expected future cash flows, expressed as a present value**.

The **cash flows** differ by asset (dividends for shares, coupons and face value for bonds, after-tax cash flows for projects). The **discount rate** reflects the **risk** of those flows: **riskier assets get higher rates**.

**Intrinsic value** is the value a neutral analyst would reach with **accurate cash flow estimates and the right discount rate**. Relative valuation and option pricing are **built on** DCF.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Four inputs are needed: expected cash flows, a risk-suited discount rate, the growth rate and the pattern of growth.

self_check.prompt_text: What determines the discount rate in DCF?

items.title: FCFE, FCFF and the discount rate
items.core_explanation_md:
**Dividend:** the only cash an equity holder actually receives. **FCFE:** cash left **after debt holders and preferred dividends are paid** and after the **reinvestment** needed for growth. **FCFF:** cash to **all** claim holders, = **after-tax operating income less net investment**.

**Discount rates:** **cost of equity** = **risk-free rate plus a premium for non-diversifiable (market) risk**; **cost of debt** reflects **default risk** and is **lower after tax** because interest is deductible; **cost of capital** = the **weighted average** of the two at **market value weights** (not book values).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Discount FCFE at the cost of equity and FCFF at the cost of capital.

self_check.prompt_text: Which weights are used in the cost of capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Market value weights of debt and equity, not book values.

items.title: Growth: estimating it and choosing a pattern
items.core_explanation_md:
**Estimating growth:** from the **company's history** (the past may mislead), from **analysts** (watch for bias) or from **surveys** of investors. **Inflation** is an input.

**Patterns:** **stable** growth, **two-stage** (high then stable) and **three-stage or n-stage** (with a transition).

**Company types:** **stable** (growth at or below the economy's nominal growth), **moderate** (just above, within about 8 to 10 per cent of the economy's growth as a rule of thumb) and **high** (well above).

**Competitive advantage:** **broad** advantages (brand, scale) **fade gradually**; **specific** ones (a patent) **end abruptly**. **Strong entry barriers, a competitive edge and capable management slow the fade.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: A two-stage model fits a patent that expires; a three-stage model fits a firm whose edge erodes slowly.

self_check.prompt_text: Which advantage ends abruptly: a brand or a patent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A patent.

items.title: Choosing a DCF approach
items.core_explanation_md:
**Can cash flows be estimated?** If **yes**: **FCFE** for a firm with **stable leverage**, **FCFF** where **leverage changes**. If **no**: use the **dividend discount model**.

**Current earnings:** **positive and normal**: use them. **Abnormal or negative but the firm survives**: use **normalised** earnings. **Survival in doubt**: value equity as an **option to liquidate** or estimate **liquidation value**.

**Present growth:** **below the economy's rate**: **stable growth model**. **Above it with a short-lived edge**: **two-stage**. **Above it with a long-lived edge**: **three-stage or n-stage**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The three decision paths can be combined: choose the cash flow, the earnings base and the growth model.

self_check.prompt_text: Which model suits a firm growing above the economy whose edge will soon fade?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The two-stage model.

items.title: Constant growth and zero growth models
items.core_explanation_md:
**Constant growth:** **P0 = D1 / (r - g)**, where **D1 = D0 x (1 + g)**. It needs **r above g**.

**Zero growth:** **P0 = D / r**, the same dividend forever.

Example: **D1 = 3, r = 12 per cent, g = 5 per cent** gives **3 / 0.07 = Rs 42.86**; with **no growth**, **3 / 0.12 = Rs 25**.

items.title: Two-stage and H models
items.core_explanation_md:
**Two-stage:** high growth **g1 for n years**, then **g2 forever**. **P0 = present value of the dividends in stage 1 + P_n / (1 + r)^n**, where **P_n = D_(n+1) / (r - g2)**.

**H model:** growth starts at **g_a** and **falls linearly** over **2H years** to **g_n**. **P0 = [D0 x (1 + g_n) + D0 x H x (g_a - g_n)] / (r - g_n)**: a **normal growth value** plus a **premium for abnormal growth**.

The H model assumes **constant payout and cost of equity** and **fails for firms paying little or no dividend**.

items.title: Three-stage dividend model
items.core_explanation_md:
The **three-stage model** has a **high growth** period, a **transition** period in which growth **declines linearly**, and a **stable** period.

It lets the **payout ratio** and **cost of equity** change from stage to stage, so it is the **most general** of the dividend models. Its **terminal value** at the end of the transition is **dividend in the first stable year / (stable cost of equity - stable growth)**, discounted back.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because it needs many inputs, it is used for companies whose growth changes substantially.

self_check.prompt_text: What may change between stages in the three-stage model?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The growth rate, the payout ratio and the cost of equity.
