items.title: Strengths and weaknesses of the dividend discount model
items.core_explanation_md:
**For:** **easy to understand**; dividends are the **only cash shareholders actually receive**; forecasting dividends needs **fewer assumptions** than forecasting free cash flow; dividends are **smoothed**, so values are **more stable**.

**Against:** it treats **dividends as if they were cash flow**. A company that **hoards cash** and pays low dividends is **undervalued**; one that pays **more than its cash flow** supports, and issues debt or stock to do so, is **overvalued**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The five forms in common use are the zero growth, constant growth, H, two-stage and three-stage models.

self_check.expected_takeaway: One that holds back cash and pays low dividends.

items.title: Relative valuation and its steps
items.core_explanation_md:
**Relative valuation** values an asset by the **prices at which comparable assets sell**, turned into **multiples**. It **complements DCF**, since most multiples rest on DCF ideas.

**Steps:** 1. **research the subject company**; 2. **identify analogous businesses** (a short list of **3 or 4** from **10 to 15** in the industry, a subjective choice); 3. **choose the multiples**; 4. **compute the multiples for the comparables**; 5. **apply the average multiples** to the subject's matching figure and **average the estimates**, adjusting for the subject's **growth, risk and size**.

**Two groups:** **equity multiples** (P/E, P/B, P/S) and **enterprise value multiples** (EV/EBITDA, EV/FCFF, EV/BV, EV/sales).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A wide spread between estimates from different multiples signals that the multiples are not equally suitable.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two enterprise value multiples.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example EV/EBITDA and EV/sales.

items.title: P/E multiple and its fundamental determinant
items.core_explanation_md:
**P/E = price per share / EPS**, usually **P0 / E1** (current price over next year's expected EPS).

**Fundamental form: P0 / E1 = (1 - b) / (r - ROE x b)**, with **(1 - b)** the **payout ratio**, **b** the **retention ratio**, **r** the **cost of equity** and **ROE x b** the **growth rate**.

**Use:** earnings power drives value; low P/E stocks have tended to do well. **Limits:** **meaningless when EPS is negative**; earnings include **one-off items**; accounting choices hamper comparison.

assumptions: Stable growth equal to ROE x b
r exceeds the growth rate
common_errors: Using the payout ratio as b
Using ROE x payout as growth

items.expanded_explanation_md: Higher payout, higher growth and lower risk all raise the justified P/E.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is P/E not usable when EPS is negative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A negative earnings figure gives a meaningless multiple.

items.title: P/B and P/S multiples
items.core_explanation_md:
**P/B = price / book value per share**, where **book value per share = (shareholders' funds - preference capital) / equity shares**. **Fundamental form: P0 / B0 = ROE x (1 - b) / (r - g)**.

**P/S = price / sales per share**; **fundamental form: P0 / S0 = NPM x (1 + g) x (1 - b) / (r - g)**.

**Why used:** **book value and sales are almost always positive**, more **stable** than EPS, and **sales are harder to manipulate**. **Limits:** **intangibles are missing from book value**; **inflation and technology** widen the gap to market; **P/S differs by industry** (margin, growth, asset turnover).

assumptions: Stable growth
r exceeds g
common_errors: Using the retention ratio in place of the payout ratio
Taking book value from a balance sheet with a large unrecorded intangible base without adjustment

items.expanded_explanation_md: A high ROE and a high payout support a high P/B; high risk (high r) lowers it.

self_check.prompt_text: Which companies suit P/B best?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Those whose balance sheets show assets near market value, such as banks.

items.title: Modified multiples: PEG, value ratio, PSM and relative P/E
items.core_explanation_md:
Each equity multiple has a **companion variable**: **growth for P/E**, **ROE for P/B**, **net profit margin for P/S**.

**Modified multiples:** **PEG = P/E / expected EPS growth rate** (**below 1** suggests **undervaluation**, **above 1** overvaluation); **value ratio = P/B / ROE**; **PSM = P/S / NPM**.

**Relative P/E = firm's P/E / market P/E**; the average across firms is **1**. Compare it with the firm's **own history** or across **markets**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Slow growers look cheap on relative P/E when market growth is high and expensive when it is low.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a PEG above 1 suggest?
self_check.expected_takeaway: That the stock may be overvalued relative to its growth.

items.title: Enterprise value multiples and their determinants
items.core_explanation_md:
**EV = market value of equity + market value of debt - cash.** Cash is netted because **interest on cash is not in EBITDA**.

**Fundamental forms:** **EV/EBITDA = (ROIC - g)(1 - DA)(1 - t) / [ROIC x (WACC - g)]**; **EV/EBIT = (1 - t)(1 - reinvestment rate) / (WACC - g)**; **EV/FCFF = 1 / (WACC - g)**; **EV/BV = (ROIC - g) / (WACC - g)**; **EV/Sales = after-tax operating margin x (1 + g) x (1 - reinvestment rate) / (WACC - g)**.

**EBITDA** is a rough proxy for free cash flow but more **stable** than FCFF, which is why **EV/EBITDA** is popular.

variables.name: Free cash flow to the firm next year

assumptions: Stable growth
WACC exceeds g
common_errors: Adding cash to enterprise value
Using equity value where enterprise value is needed

items.expanded_explanation_md: EV multiples value the business itself, so debt is deducted afterwards to get equity value.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is cash netted in EV/EBITDA?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest income on cash is not in EBITDA, so leaving cash in would overstate the multiple.

items.title: Choosing the right multiple
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three views:** **cynical** (pick the multiple that gives the answer you want, which is poor practice), **bludgeon** (use **all** multiples: a range, a **simple** or a **weighted** average) and **best multiple**.

**Matching multiple to company:** **P/E**: positive earnings record, no large non-cash charges. **PEG**: stable earnings growth and risk. **P/B**: assets near market value, as in **banks**. **EV/EBITDA**: large **non-cash expenses**, capital-intensive firms (airlines, telecom, refineries). **EV/FCFF**: stable growth and predictable capex. **EV/Sales**: **young firms** with **no profit record**.

**Best multiple by method:** **fundamental** (the variable most tied to value) or **statistical** (highest R-squared in a regression).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A simple average gives all multiples equal weight even though some are more pertinent.

self_check.prompt_text: Which multiple suits a young company with no profit record?
self_check.expected_takeaway: EV/sales.

items.title: Book value, NAV and the stock and debt approach
items.core_explanation_md:
**Book value** = **investor claims** (share capital + reserves + loans) = **total assets less current liabilities and provisions**.

**It differs from market value** because of **inflation**, **obsolescence** and unrecorded **organisational capital**.

**NAV = value of assets at replacement or market value (including investments and cash) less outstanding debt; NAV per share = NAV / number of shares.**

**Problems:** assets may be **thinly traded**, markets can be **inefficient**, value **in use** differs from market value, **intangibles** are hard to value and **synergy** is missed.

**Stock and debt approach: market value of equity + market value of debt.** The **unadjusted book value** suits only unusual cases such as **regulated industries**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The liquidation approach ignores organisational capital and is meaningful only for a firm worth more dead than alive.

self_check.prompt_text: How is NAV per share found?
self_check.expected_takeaway: NAV, being assets at market or replacement value less debt, divided by the number of equity shares.

items.title: Intangible assets and how to value them
items.core_explanation_md:
**Intangibles** (goodwill, brand, skilled people, technology) are often **understated or ignored** in accounts.

**Cash-flow-generating intangibles** (patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, **franchises**): value the **cash flows from the exclusive right over its finite life**, usually with **no terminal value**, by **DCF** or a **multiple** from comparable assets. Reduce value for **enforcement costs** and **infringement**.

**Brand name and similar:** **capital investment** (capitalise past spend, such as advertising; **least subjective** but far from market value), **DCF** (the **extra cash flow** attributable to the asset) or **relative** (compare firms **with and without** the brand).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A franchisee pays an initial charge and an annual fee in return for the brand, support and advertising.

self_check.prompt_text: Which approach to valuing a brand is the least subjective?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The capital investment approach, which capitalises past spending.

items.title: Valuing real estate firms
items.core_explanation_md:
Real and financial assets share the principle that **value depends on cash flows, growth and risk**, so **intrinsic and relative valuation** apply.

**Differences:** **buildings have a finite life**, but **land lasts for ever** and can dominate the **terminal value**.

**Cost of equity:** use **CAPM or multifactor models**. Critics say property investors are **not diversified**; the courseware replies that concentration is a **choice**, property can be **subdivided and securitised**, and **diversified institutions** (REITs, partnerships) are likely to be the **marginal investors**. **Beta** for real assets is hard to measure for lack of a **price history** against an index.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The value of the land component may matter more than the building in the final value.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can land dominate the terminal value of a real estate firm?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because land has an endless life while buildings wear out.

items.title: Valuing a start-up: reinvestment and survival
items.core_explanation_md:
**Information is thin**, so use the **latest twelve months**, peer margins and bottom-up betas.

**Reinvestment when earnings are negative:** **expected reinvestment = expected change in revenue / (sales-to-capital ratio)**. A ratio of **5** means **Rs 2 lakh of capital for each Rs 10 lakh of extra revenue**.

**Growth** (when earnings are positive): **expected growth = reinvestment rate x return on capital**; in **stable growth**: **reinvestment rate = stable growth / stable ROC**.

**Survival:** **value of firm = P(survive) x DCF value + (1 - P(survive)) x distress or liquidation value.**

**Terminal value** holds most of the value, so the **growth and margin assumptions** matter most.

items.expanded_explanation_md: Cash balances of young firms burn fast, so recent figures matter; options outstanding must be valued and deducted before dividing by shares.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The sales-to-capital ratio.

items.title: Negative or low earnings: the cause decides the treatment
items.core_explanation_md:
| Cause | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| **Temporary** (strike, recall) or **one-off** | Remove the cost, use **normalised earnings** (mind the tax effect) |
| **Cyclical or industry-wide** | Use **normalised earnings** |
| **Long-term problems** (obsolete plant, poor investment) | Judge **whether and when** they can be solved |
| **Strategic blunders** (the courseware cites Kodak, IBM, Xerox) | **Cut revenue growth and margin** expectations |
| **Operating inefficiency** | **Raise margin towards the industry average**; speed depends on **size**, **type of inefficiency**, **external limits** and **management quality** |

For **heavily indebted** firms also consider the **risk of default**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A large firm needs a larger absolute cost cut for the same margin gain, so correcting inefficiency takes longer.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does firm size slow the correction of inefficiency?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The absolute scale of the change needed is greater and organisational inertia is stronger.

items.title: Financial service companies: dividend model inputs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Special features:** **debt is the raw material**, so debt and reinvestment are hard to define; **heavy regulation and capital adequacy norms**; **loan loss provisioning**; **difficulty choosing multiples**.

**Inputs for the dividend model:** **bottom-up beta** (average levered beta of comparables); **payout ratio including buybacks** (use a **composite over several years**); **growth = retention ratio x ROE**; with changing ROE: **retention x ROE(t+1) + (ROE(t+1) - ROE(t)) / ROE(t)**.

**Stable growth:** **payout ratio = 1 - g / ROE(stable)**, with beta moving towards 1.

variables.name: Return on equity in stable growth

assumptions: Growth equals retention x ROE in stable growth
common_errors: Using the high-growth payout in the stable stage
Ignoring buybacks when computing payout

items.expanded_explanation_md: Banks pay higher dividends than most firms because regulation leaves them lower net capital expenditure and investors expect reliable payouts.

self_check.prompt_text: Why compute a composite payout including buybacks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because buybacks vary year to year, so dividends alone misstate the cash returned to shareholders.

items.title: Asset-based valuation of a financial institution
items.core_explanation_md:
Value the **loan portfolio** at **fair market value**: the **present value of its coupons at the market rate plus the present value of the principal**. Then **deduct deposits, debt and other claims** to get the **equity**.

A loan book earning **more than the market rate** is worth **more than book value**.

**Drawbacks:** it ignores **future growth and excess returns**, and it is **hard for firms in many businesses** (insurance, banking, investment banking) at once.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A loan paying above the going rate has a fair value above face value.

self_check.prompt_text: When is a loan worth more than its face value?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When its coupon rate exceeds the current market rate for similar risk.

items.title: Equity as a call option in distressed firms
items.core_explanation_md:
For a **distressed** firm with large debt, equity holders have **limited liability** and the option to **liquidate**.

**Payoff to equity = V - D if V > D; 0 if V is at most D**, where **V** is the firm value and **D** the **face value of debt and other claims**. The **exercise price** is the **debt's face value**; the option **expires when the debt matures**.

**Implications:** equity can have value **even when V is below D** (time value), and **higher risk can raise equity value**, unlike in DCF.

variables.name: Face value of debt and other non-equity claims

assumptions: Limited liability
Debt falls due at a set date
common_errors: Allowing a negative equity value
Assuming risk always lowers equity value

items.expanded_explanation_md: This is why a firm with negative net worth can still have a positive share price.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can higher risk raise the value of equity in a distressed firm?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Equity holders have little to lose and much to gain, like the holder of an option.

items.title: Cash, cross holdings and consolidated versus separate valuation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Non-operating assets:** **cash and near-cash**, **stakes in other firms**, **idle land**, **surplus pension assets**.

**Why hold cash (Keynes):** **transactions**, **precaution**, **speculation**; also **managers may hoard**. Cash needs are **higher for cash businesses** (restaurants), **lower for firms with large transactions** and fall with **digital payments**.

**Consolidated valuation:** cash **inside** the firm: earnings include **interest on cash**; beta is the **weighted average** of operating assets and cash; **do not add cash again**.

**Separate valuation:** **operating assets only**; **exclude interest on cash**; **add cash** to the value of operations.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Both routes should give the same value if applied consistently.

self_check.prompt_text: Under separate valuation, what is done with cash?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is excluded from operations and added to the value of the operating assets.

items.title: Warrants and convertibles
items.core_explanation_md:
A **convertible bond or preferred share** carries a **call option** to convert into equity at a **fixed price**.

Because its value **depends on the equity value**, it **cannot simply be deducted as debt** from enterprise value. If an **offer price exceeds the conversion price**, treating all convertibles as **converted** is reasonable.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Their value is found with option pricing methods.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a convertible not be treated purely as debt?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Its value depends on the company equity value through the conversion option.

items.title: Cyclical firms: normalising earnings
items.core_explanation_md:
Earnings in the **base year** can mislead for cyclical firms. **Remedies:** **adjust expected growth** (for example **higher near-term growth** when earnings are depressed), or **normalise earnings**: **what would the firm earn in a typical year?**

**Methods:** **average earnings over a full cycle** (**five to ten years**); **average the ROC or margin** over past periods and **apply it to current capital or revenue**, which adjusts for **current size** (revenue-based margins are **harder to manipulate**); and if recovery takes **several periods**, **reduce value for the delay**.

**Normalised earnings = average return on capital x current capital.**

variables.name: Average return on capital over the cycle

assumptions: The past cycle is representative
common_errors: Averaging rupee earnings for a firm whose size changed
Assuming normalisation is immediate when recovery will take years

items.expanded_explanation_md: Holding companies are valued with FCF and dividend models and for their investment ability; e-commerce firms by looking at technology, buyer habits and competition.

self_check.prompt_text: Why average a margin rather than rupee earnings for a firm that has grown?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A margin applied to current revenue reflects the present size, while old rupee earnings come from a smaller firm.

items.title: Types of mergers, acquisitions and takeovers
items.core_explanation_md:
| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Horizontal merger** | Firms in the **same market** combine: **larger market share**, possible **near-monopoly** |
| **Vertical merger** | **Buyer and seller** (supplier and customer) combine |
| **Conglomerate merger** | **Unconnected businesses**; gains come from **financial resources, debt capacity, management** |
| **Congeneric merger** | Firms **connected** by technology, products or markets |
| **Reverse merger** | A **smaller unlisted** firm acquires a **larger listed** one, avoiding a lengthy **public issue** |

**Acquisition:** purchase of a **controlling interest** (by agreement, fresh shares, open market, cash plus shares, or a general offer). **Slump sale:** a business sold for **one lump sum** without values for each asset. **Purchase of a division or plant:** only **part** of a firm is bought. **Takeover:** acquiring a stake, typically **50 to 100 per cent**, to gain **control**; **friendly** if the target management agrees, **hostile** if not. **Leveraged buyout:** a takeover **financed mainly by debt**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a merger two firms become one; in an acquisition one firm buys control of another that may continue as a separate company.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of merger joins a supplier and its customer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A vertical merger.

items.title: Why firms merge: synergy and economies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Synergy:** the combined value exceeds the separate values, **V(AB) > V(A) + V(B)**.

**Real gains:** **operating economies** (**real** economies cut inputs per unit of output; **pecuniary** ones come from **cheaper factor prices**), **economies of scale and scope**, **vertical integration** (but **outsourcing** may be better), **complementary resources**, **faster growth** and shorter **time to market**, **market power** from fewer competitors, **tax** benefits such as set-off of losses, **use of surplus funds**, **managerial effectiveness** (a better team, and the **threat of takeover** disciplines managers) and **industry consolidation** where capacity is excessive.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Buying a ready business can be faster than building plant and hiring staff from scratch.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the condition for synergy in a merger of A and B?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The combined value is greater than the sum of the separate values.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Dubious reasons for merging
items.core_explanation_md:
**Diversification:** investors can **diversify cheaply** by holding shares in both firms, so a merger adds **no value for them**. **Exceptions:** a firm facing **bankruptcy** that only a merger can save, and a firm whose **owners cannot diversify** by themselves.

**Lower financing costs:** each firm creditors become a **guarantor of the other**, so **shareholders bear extra risk**; in an efficient market the **lower cost of debt is offset by a higher cost of equity**.

**Growth in earnings per share:** the **P/E ratio of the combined firm falls**, so its **market value is the sum of the separate values** and the rise in **EPS is an illusion**. Only an **inefficient** market can be fooled.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Earnings per share can rise through a merger even though no value has been created.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a rise in EPS after a merger not prove value was created?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The price-earnings ratio of the combined firm falls, so market value stays at the sum of the separate values.

items.title: How an amalgamation proceeds, and the regulators
items.core_explanation_md:
**Regulators:** the **Companies Act** (main law; **NCLT** sanctions the scheme), **SEBI** (protects **minority shareholders**), the **Competition Commission** (protects **consumers** from reduced competition; combinations above specified limits must be **notified**).

**Sequence:** review **object clauses** -> inform **stock exchanges** -> **board approvals** of the draft scheme -> **application to the NCLT** -> **notice** to shareholders and creditors -> **meetings** where a prescribed majority in value must approve -> **petition to the NCLT** to confirm -> file the order with the **Registrar** -> **transfer of assets and liabilities** -> **issue of shares and debentures**, after which trading begins.

**Investment bankers** arrange mergers, develop **defences**, determine **fair value**, **finance** the deal and run **arbitrage**. The specific majorities, notice periods and thresholds are **not taught** here.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Fair value matters because shareholders can challenge a price that is not reasonable.

self_check.prompt_text: Which body sanctions an amalgamation scheme?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The National Company Law Tribunal.

items.title: Tax and accounting for business combinations
items.core_explanation_md:
**Tax:** a qualifying amalgamation lets the combined firm claim certain **deductions** and **carry forward unabsorbed losses and depreciation**; **stamp duty** is a **state** levy. Conditions and figures are **not taught**.

**Accounting under Ind AS 103: acquisition method**

1. **Identify the acquirer.**
2. Determine the **acquisition date**.
3. **Recognise and measure** identifiable assets, liabilities and any **non-controlling interest** at **fair value**.
4. Recognise **goodwill** or a **gain on a bargain purchase**.

**Common control combinations** (the same party controls all combining entities before and after): the **pooling of interests** method uses **carrying amounts**, makes **no fair value adjustments**, and adjusts the **difference in capital** from the share exchange in **reserves**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Under pooling no new goodwill appears, because values are not restated.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The pooling of interests method.

items.title: Merger gain and cost with cash compensation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Benefit** = **PV(AB) - (PV(A) + PV(B))**.

**Cash:** **cost = cash paid - PV(B)**; **NPV to A = benefit - cost = PV(AB) - PV(A) - cash**; **NPV to B = cash - PV(B)**.

Example pattern: if the total gain is **Rs 25 crore** and A pays **Rs 5 crore above B stand-alone value**, A keeps **Rs 20 crore** and B gets **Rs 5 crore**. The gain is **shared**; **a higher price moves gain from A to B**.

assumptions: Cash paid is certain and independent of the merger gain
Values are present values
common_errors: Comparing cash with the target market price instead of its stand-alone value
Forgetting that the cash paid is the acquirer cost

items.expanded_explanation_md: The seller gains only if the cash exceeds its stand-alone value.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the cost of a cash merger to the acquirer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The cash paid minus the stand-alone value of the target.

items.title: Merger cost with stock compensation
items.core_explanation_md:
Target holders receive a **fraction alpha of the combined firm**: **alpha = new shares issued / (acquirer shares + new shares issued)**.

**True cost = alpha x PV(AB) - PV(B)**, where **PV(AB) = PV(A) + PV(B) + benefit**.

The **apparent cost** (**shares issued x acquirer price**, minus PV(B)) **understates** the true cost because target holders **share in the gain**. **NPV to A = benefit - cost**; **NPV to B = cost**.

**With stock, the cost depends on the merger gain; with cash it does not.**

variables.name: Fraction of the combined firm owned by target holders
Value of the combined firm including the benefit

assumptions: Shares are valued at their pre-merger market values
The benefit is shared in proportion to ownership
common_errors: Using the pre-merger share price to compute cost and ignoring the gain
Dividing new shares by the old share count only

items.expanded_explanation_md: Paying in stock shares the risk that the benefit will not materialise.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the apparent cost of a stock deal too low?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the target holders also own part of the merger gain.

| **Discipline** | **Cash-financed** purchases have **done better** than stock-financed ones, possibly because cash buyers are **more disciplined** |

items.title: Exchange ratio and its bases
items.core_explanation_md:
**Exchange (swap) ratio = acquirer shares offered per target share.** A ratio of **0.5** means **one acquirer share for every two target shares**.

**Ratio on a basis = value per share of the target / value per share of the acquirer**, using:

- **Book value per share**: objective, but **accounting policies and inflation** distort it.
- **Earnings per share**: ignores **unequal growth, one-off items, risk and negative earnings**.
- **Market price per share**: **current and competitive**, but **thin trading** or interested parties can distort it.
- **Dividend discount value**: suits firms with **reasonable dividend streams**.
- **DCF value per share** = (**DCF firm value - debt**) / **shares**: needs **five to ten years** of sound plans.

**New shares to issue = ratio x target shares.**

variables.name: Value per share of the target on the chosen basis
Value per share of the acquirer on the same basis

assumptions: Same basis for both firms
Values are per equity share
common_errors: Dividing the acquirer value by the target value
Mixing bases for the two firms

items.expanded_explanation_md: Different bases give different ratios, so the final ratio is a negotiated figure.

self_check.prompt_text: What does an exchange ratio of 0.5 mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The acquirer offers one share for every two target shares.

items.title: Valuing a division or plant to be bought
items.core_explanation_md:
The buyer values **three layers**:

1. **Status quo value** by **DCF** (an **explicit forecast** of five to ten years, then a **horizon value** in steady state, both discounted) or by **market multiples** of comparable assets (for example **value to NOPAT**).
2. **Value of control** = **value if optimally managed - value under current management**; large when the business is **badly run**.
3. **Value of synergy**: lower **overheads**, faster or **longer growth**, **lower cost of capital** from more debt capacity, better use of **tax**; **easy to describe, hard to value**.

**Bias:** each side wants to **justify its view**; the choice of **growth, return on capital and discount rate** can be tailored to reach a figure, especially in a **hostile** bid.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Control is worth nothing if the firm is already managed as well as it can be.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the value of control measured?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The value if optimally managed minus the value under current management.

items.title: Takeovers: routes, arguments and regulation principles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Control** can need **less than 50 per cent** (**30 to 40 per cent** if other holders are dispersed).

**Routes:** **open market purchase** (usual start of a **hostile** bid), **negotiated purchase** from promoters, **preferential allotment** (friendly; gives a **strategic stake** and brings in **funds**).

**For:** better **management quality**, **discipline** on weak managers, **synergy**, protection of **small holders**. **Against:** a focus on **size** and **short-term gain**, **raiders** seeking a quick profit, duty to **society**. **Research** quoted: **target holders gain**, bidders do **not lose**.

**Principles of regulation:** **transparency**, **minority protection** (equitable exit price), **freedom to realise economic gains**, **no undue concentration of market power**, and **financial support** for capable bidders.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A hostile takeover often starts with quiet purchases of shares on the market.

self_check.prompt_text: Which takeover route is friendly and can bring funds into the target?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A preferential allotment of shares to the acquirer.

items.title: Market concentration: the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index
items.core_explanation_md:
**HHI = the sum of the squares of the market shares**, with shares in **percentage points**.

Example pattern: **three firms with 20 per cent each and ten with 4 per cent each** give **3 x 400 + 10 x 16 = 1,360**. A market with **one firm at 52 per cent and twelve at 4 per cent** gives **2,704 + 192 = 2,896**.

The index **rises with both inequality of shares and fewer firms**, so regulators use it to judge whether a merger **concentrates market power** too much.

assumptions: Shares are expressed in percentage points
All firms in the market are included
common_errors: Adding shares instead of squares
Using fractions instead of percentage points and mixing scales

items.expanded_explanation_md: A single firm with 100 per cent share gives the maximum value of 10,000.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a merger of two large rivals raise the HHI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Their shares add and the squared sum is larger than the sum of the separate squares.

items.title: Takeover code principles and anti-takeover defences
items.core_explanation_md:
**Takeover code (principles only; percentages, days and formulae are not taught):** **disclosure** once holdings cross a stated level; a **trigger point** after which a **public offer** must be made; a **merchant banker** responsible for the offer; a **public announcement**; an **offer price** from **pricing guidelines**; an **escrow** deposit to **ensure payment**; **target board restrictions** during the offer; **competing bids**; limits on **creeping acquisition**.

**Pre-offer defences:** **staggered board**, **super-majority clause**, **poison pill**, **poison put**, **dual-class shares**, **golden parachute**.

**Post-offer defences:** **greenmail**, **Pacman defence**, **litigation**, **selling the crown jewels**, **restructuring liabilities**.

**Indian list:** **preferential allotment to promoters**, **creeping enhancement**, **amalgamated group**, **selling crown jewels**, **a white knight**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A white knight is a friendly rescuer that buys the target on better terms than the hostile bidder.

items.title: Leveraged buyouts and acquisition financing
items.core_explanation_md:
**LBO:** a company or unit is bought **mainly with debt**; a **management buyout (MBO)** is one where **management buys**. Afterwards the firm usually becomes **private**.

**Debt disciplines:** it forces **cash flow improvement**. In the courseware phrase, **debt is a sword, equity a pillow**.

**Value is created by:** **operating improvement**, **cash flow repaying debt** (raising the **equity share** of enterprise value) and the **interest tax shield**.

**Good LBO candidate:** **good management**, **steady cash flows**, **room to improve efficiency**, **assets that can be sold**, **low capital expenditure** needs and an **easy exit**.

**Acquisition finance:** lenders look at the **cash flow of the acquirer**; the courseware indicates **debt of three to six times EBITDA** at a cost **above normal financing**, depending on product and management quality, regulation and cash flow viability.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The risk is that heavy fixed charges can sink the firm if cash flow disappoints.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three sources of value in a leveraged buyout.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Operating improvement, debt paydown from cash flow and the interest tax shield.

items.title: Business alliances as an alternative to merger
items.core_explanation_md:
**Forms:** **joint ventures**, **strategic alliances**, **equity partnerships**, **licensing**, **franchising** and **network alliances**.

**Why:** **share risk and resources** (especially in **high technology**), **enter emerging markets** through a partner **channels**, **reduce expenditure** by sharing facilities, a **more favourable view from regulators** than a merger, and a **route to acquire or exit** a business.

**Success factors:** **complementary strengths**, a cost **too large for one firm**, ability to **work together**, clear **purpose, roles and obligations**, **fair sharing** of responsibilities and benefits, and comparable **time horizons** and **financial expectations**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An alliance can be a trial before a full merger.

self_check.expected_takeaway: For example complementary strengths and a fair sharing of benefits and responsibilities.

items.title: Managing acquisitions: five sins and a disciplined programme
items.core_explanation_md:
**Many deals fail to create value**, often over **people and culture**.

**Collective wisdom:** deals cluster when **markets are strong**; **buyers usually overpay**; **repeat acquirers** do better; **private targets** and **related** acquisitions do better; **integration is hard**.

**Five sins:** **wandering too far from the core**; **striving for greatness** (size over value); **plunging without thinking** (overstated intangibles, window-dressed statements, ignored contingent liabilities); **overpaying** (the **winner curse**); **inability to integrate**.

**Disciplined programme:** focus on the **right targets** (screening criteria and a database), **estimate synergies accurately**, **negotiate with discipline** (one team values, another negotiates; set a **walk-away price**) and **plan and control integration**. Premiums run **20 to 60 per cent** of pre-bid market value (courseware range).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Synergy that is only assumed, never planned, usually does not appear.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the winner curse?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The highest bidder is often the one that most overestimated the value, so it overpays.

items.title: Divestitures: forms and motives
items.core_explanation_md:
**Divestiture** is the opposite of acquisition: a **smaller asset base and less control**.

| Form | Key feature |
| --- | --- |
| **Partial sell-off** | A part of the business sold to another firm |
| **Transfer of ownership** | An investor sells an **equity stake or controlling block** |
| **Spin-off** | **Existing shareholders get shares** of the new company **pro rata**; **ownership unchanged**; **no cash raised** |
| **Split-up** | The company divides into **several independent companies**; the **parent ceases to exist** |
| **Equity carve-out** | **Part of the subsidiary equity is sold to new investors**; **cash comes in**; the **parent keeps control** |
| **Demerger** | A **legal scheme** moving undertakings to a **resulting company** |
| **PSU disinvestment** | **Government** stake transferred by **privatisation** |

**Motives:** **focus**, a division that **contributes too little**, a business **too large to manage**, **need for funds**, **strategic fit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A spin-off gives shareholders new shares; a carve-out sells shares for cash.

self_check.prompt_text: Which divestiture raises cash while the parent keeps control?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An equity carve-out.

items.title: Financial evaluation of a sell-off
items.core_explanation_md:
1. Estimate the **after-tax cash flows** of the division.
2. Choose a **discount rate for the division risk** (use firms in the **same line of business** as proxy).
3. Compute the **present value of the division**.
4. Find the **market value of the division-specific liabilities** (may differ from book value).
5. **VOP (value of ownership position) = value of the division - value of its liabilities.**
6. Compare with the **divestiture proceeds (DP)**.

**Decision rule:** **DP > VOP: sell**; **DP = VOP: indifferent**; **DP < VOP: keep.**

Market value of the division-specific liabilities

assumptions: Discount rate reflects the division risk
Liabilities are valued at market, not book
common_errors: Using book value of liabilities
Using the parent discount rate for a division of different risk

items.expanded_explanation_md: The parent sells only when the proceeds beat what the division is worth to it.

self_check.prompt_text: If divestiture proceeds are below VOP, what should the parent do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Keep the division.

items.title: Holding companies and demergers
items.core_explanation_md:
**Holding company:** owns **equity in other companies** to **control** them; **full ownership is not needed**, and control may be possible with **as little as 25 per cent** if relations with other holders are managed (courseware).

**Benefits:** **central control**, **flexibility for growth**, **succession planning**, **tax planning**, **risk mitigation**, **legal protection of group assets**, **optimum use of funds**.

**Demerger:** a **legal scheme** moving **one or more undertakings** into a **resulting company**; the **demerged company** transfers. **Family groups** use it to **divide a business empire** and solve **succession**.

**Tax-neutral demerger (courseware conditions):** the resulting company takes **all assets and liabilities** of the undertaking **at the book values** of the demerged company, issues **shares to the demerged company shareholders in proportion**, and a **required proportion** of shareholders move across (**not taught**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a demerger the shareholders end up holding shares in both companies.

self_check.expected_takeaway: It receives the transferred undertaking and issues shares to the demerged company shareholders.

items.title: Deal structure and the negotiation
items.core_explanation_md:
A **deal structure** is the **agreement between acquirer and target** on their **rights and obligations**, reached by **negotiation** after the strategy, target choice and financial analysis are done.

Structuring decides **how risk is shared** and how many of each party goals are met, including **how much of the target liabilities the acquirer takes on**. **Risk moved out of one place tends to reappear in another** (the courseware image is **squeezing a water balloon**).

**Main aspects:** the **acquisition vehicle and post-closing organisation**, the **form of acquisition**, the **form of payment** and the **legal form of the seller**. **Financing, tax and structure are interwoven**, and **private equity and hedge funds** often help finance leveraged deals. The aim is a **mutually beneficial (win-win)** outcome.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A deal that looks cheap but leaves all risk with one side is unlikely to close.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a deal structure specify?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The rights and obligations of the acquirer and the target, including how risk is shared.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Advanced Business & Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-774-0

items.title: Choosing the acquisition vehicle and post-closing organisation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Consideration** can be **cash, stock, debt or a mix**, as a **lump sum**, tied to future performance (**earn-out**) or **paid over time**.

**Factors in the choice of vehicle:** **cost and formality**, **ease of transferring ownership**, **continuity**, **management control**, **ease of raising finance**, **ease of assimilation**, **distribution of earnings**, **personal liability** and **tax**.

**Corporate structure** is the most used: **limited liability**, **continuity**, **flexible financing**. An **ESOP** can sell a small private business to **employees** with tax benefits.

**Post-closing options:** a **corporate or divisional** structure gives the **most control and quick integration**; **joint ventures and partnerships** **slow decisions**. A **holding company** isolates **target liabilities**, suits **earn-outs**, **foreign targets** and **financial investors**. A **partnership or LLP** passes **losses and credits** to owners but may bring **double taxation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The best vehicle depends on which risk and tax attributes the buyer most wants to keep.

self_check.prompt_text: Why might an acquirer use a holding company for a target with large liabilities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It can isolate the obligations in the subsidiary so that the parent is protected from the target bankruptcy.

items.title: Paying in cash or in stock
items.core_explanation_md:
| Cash is favoured when | Stock is favoured when |
| --- | --- |
| The **acquirer wants control** and no **dilution** | The acquirer thinks the **target is overvalued** |
| The acquirer has **high credit rating and cheap borrowing** or **large cash** | The acquirer has **limited borrowing capacity** or its **leverage is already high** |
| The target has **large borrowing capacity** or **cheap shares** | The acquirer needs **cash for integration** spending |
|  | The **target value is hard to judge** (intangibles, new products): the **seller shares upside and downside** |

items.title: Mixed offers, proration and convertibles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Mixed offers** attract more target holders because some prefer **cash** (to pay tax) and others **stock**. A **choice** makes the **total cash needed unpredictable**.

**Proration clause:** if elections for cash exceed the **cash pool**, each electing holder receives **cash pool / cash elected** as a fraction of the cash requested, the rest in stock.

**Convertibles** help when **both sides lack information**: they give the target holders a **floor value** (**debt value at maturity plus accrued interest**) and a **share of future upside** if the price rises above the **conversion price**; otherwise they stay **debt**.

**Conversion ratio = face value / conversion price**; **conversion value = ratio x current share price**.

items.title: Tax considerations and the shape of the deal
items.core_explanation_md:
**The core economics decide the deal; tax benefits only reinforce it.** The **buyer** cares about the **tax basis of acquired assets** and **hidden tax liabilities**; the **seller** about **postponing tax**.

**Taxable to target holders:** most of the consideration is **cash, debt or other non-equity**: **cash purchase of assets or shares**, **cash statutory merger**.

**Triangular merger:** the target is combined with an **acquirer subsidiary**, shielding the **acquirer from the target liabilities**: **forward** (target merges into the subsidiary) or **reverse** (subsidiary merges into the target).

**Asset purchase:** **step-up** of asset basis to **fair market value** gives **extra depreciation and lower later tax**, but the seller may face **double taxation** (company tax, then tax on distributing the proceeds).

**Stock purchase:** **no company-level tax** and **no step-up** unless elected.

**Tax-free (courseware, United States rules):** **mainly acquirer stock**, **continuity of ownership**, **continuity of business**, a **legitimate business purpose**. Non-equity consideration (**boot**) is taxed. **Tax losses** may be used by the acquirer subject to limits.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A tax saving that is the only reason for a deal can make the deal fail the tests for tax-free treatment.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the main benefit to the buyer of a taxable asset purchase?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The assets are stepped up to fair value, giving more depreciation and lower tax later.

items.title: Tax reliefs for amalgamations in India (principles)
items.core_explanation_md:
For an amalgamation that meets the **statutory conditions**:

- **No capital gains** arise on **transfer of assets** to the **Indian amalgamated company**.
- **Shareholders** swapping shares for shares of the Indian amalgamated company are **exempt from capital gains** on the exchange.
- **Accumulated losses and unabsorbed depreciation** carry forward **only for specified undertakings** and **only if conditions** on **continuing the business** and **use of assets** are met; otherwise the benefit is **withdrawn**.
- The courseware notes **no express provision** to carry forward **MAT credit** to the amalgamated company.

**Issues:** **cash or securities** paid to holders and **part payment to demerged company holders**. **Cross-border:** **double taxation** arises when two countries tax the same income; **DTAAs** reduce it but can be **amended**.

**Sections, percentages and periods are not taught.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: The reliefs exist to stop a genuine reorganisation from being taxed as a sale.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do double taxation avoidance agreements matter in cross-border deals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They limit the overlapping claims of two countries to tax the same income.

items.title: Acquisition method: goodwill and non-controlling interest
items.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** identify the **acquirer**; fix the **acquisition date**; recognise and measure **identifiable assets, liabilities and any non-controlling interest (NCI)**; recognise **goodwill or a bargain purchase gain**.

**Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI - fair value of identifiable net assets** (if positive). If **negative**, it is a **gain from a bargain purchase**.

**Consolidation shows 100 per cent** of the target **assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses**, even when the acquirer buys **50.1 per cent**. The **part not owned** appears as **NCI in equity**, and **profit attributable to NCI** is shown separately.

In a **share acquisition** the target standalone books do not record intangibles; the **consolidated statements** record them at **acquisition-date fair value**.

items.title: Financing a deal: sources and debt features
items.core_explanation_md:
**Choice of finance** depends on **capital market state**, **liquidity and credit standing** of both firms, **combined borrowing capacity**, **deal size** and **target holders preference**.

**Sources:** **equity or preference shares**, **internal accruals**, **long-term bank loans**, **convertible or non-convertible debentures** and other **domestic or foreign debt**.

**Decoupling:** an acquirer can **raise equity beforehand** from investors told that the proceeds will finance acquisitions; issuing when **shares are richly valued** helps.

**Debt:** gives an **interest tax shield** and **often higher EPS and ROE**, but **too much** raises **distress risk** and **limits flexibility**. **Merging firms with uncorrelated cash flows** can carry **more debt** afterwards.

**Senior debt** ranks ahead of **subordinated (junior)** debt, which is **unsecured**. **Convertible** bonds convert at a **set ratio**, usually carry a **lower coupon** and **dilute** owners on conversion. The **indenture** sets out **repayment, affirmative and negative covenants**. **Rating** depends on **earnings consistency, interest cover, debt to total capital, subordination and repayment history**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Seniority matters because it decides who is paid first if the combined firm fails.

self_check.prompt_text: What is an indenture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The contract setting out how the debt will be repaid and the covenants the borrower must observe.

items.title: Comparing financing by equity and by debt
items.core_explanation_md:
**After-tax cost of debt = interest rate x (1 - tax rate).**

**EPS with equity financing** = **(earnings) / (existing shares + new shares)**, where **new shares = amount raised / issue price**.

**EPS with debt financing** = **(earnings - interest x (1 - tax rate)) / existing shares**.

**Interest cover = EBIT / interest.**

Debt often gives the **higher EPS**, but **cover falls** and **risk rises**. EPS alone is not a test of value.

items.title: Financing cross-border and domestic acquisitions in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Inbound** (foreign acquirer, Indian target): the loan market is **mostly overseas**. A common route is an **offshore SPV** that **borrows abroad** and **invests via foreign direct investment**. A **foreign owned and controlled company (FOCC)** in India **cannot leverage domestically** to buy shares, so it issues **non-convertible debentures (NCDs)** to **foreign portfolio investors**.

**Outbound** (Indian acquirer, foreign target): **domestic funds** (subject to central bank rules), **external commercial borrowing**, or an **offshore SPV** borrowing from offshore lenders.

**Domestic:** mainly **NCDs** and **loans from non-banking finance companies and funds**.

Cross-border loan agreements often follow **market standard forms** (the **LMA** or **APLMA**). **Specific limits, eligibility and rules are not taught**; they change and must be checked at the time.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The same acquisition can be financed through several different routes, each with its own rules.

self_check.expected_takeaway: To raise finance in overseas markets against its own assets and then invest in the Indian target.

items.title: Hybrid securities: meaning, types, advantages and drawbacks
items.core_explanation_md:
A **hybrid security** combines **debt and equity features** in one instrument, giving **flexibility to postpone payment** and letting the issuer tune its **debt-equity mix**.

**Types:** **preference shares**, **warrants**, **convertible debentures or bonds**, **foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCB)**, **mezzanine financing**.

| Advantages | Disadvantage |
| --- | --- |
| **Higher yield than debt** | **Hard to assess**: return is **not as simple to calculate** as on equity or bonds |
| **Less price volatility than equity** (regular, pre-determined return) |  |
| **Risk diversification** for the issuer (**no strict definition** as debt or equity) |  |

A hybrid is **innovative** when its reward is **linked to an economic variable** such as an **interest rate, exchange rate or commodity index**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Hybrids sit between the two extremes of debt and equity on the financing spectrum.

self_check.prompt_text: What makes a hybrid security innovative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Its reward is linked to a general economic variable such as an interest rate, exchange rate or commodities index.

items.title: Preference share capital
items.core_explanation_md:
**Preference shareholders** have a **priority claim** over equity holders on **income** (a **fixed-rate dividend** paid **before** equity) and on **assets** in **liquidation**.

**But:** they have **no legal right to force payment** and **cannot push the company into bankruptcy** for a missed dividend.

**Companies Act idea:** capital with a **preferential right to a fixed dividend** and to **repayment of capital on winding up** is **preference capital**; extra participation rights do not change that.

Preference shares may be **issued with or without maturity**; **perpetual (irredeemable)** shares have none. **Classes** can be **senior or junior** to each other. **Rating agencies** can rate them.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Preference capital ranks after all creditors but before equity.

self_check.prompt_text: Can preference shareholders force a company into bankruptcy for a missed dividend?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, they have no legal right to compel payment of the dividend.

items.title: Kinds of preference shares
items.core_explanation_md:
| Kind | Feature |
| --- | --- |
| **Cumulative** | **Unpaid dividends accumulate** (arrears) and must be paid **before any equity dividend** |
| **Non-cumulative** | A **missed dividend is lost**; no arrears |
| **Participating** | **Fixed dividend plus a share in surplus profits** after equity holders get a stated rate (and surplus on winding up) |
| **Non-participating** | **Only the fixed dividend** and the **preference amount** on winding up |
| **Redeemable** | **Repaid** after a set period or earlier at the **issuer option** |
| **Non-redeemable** | Repaid only on **liquidation** |
| **Convertible** | Can be **converted to equity** at the holder option |
| **Non-convertible** | **No conversion right** unless stated |
| **Adjustable-rate** | Dividend **linked to market interest rates**, not fixed |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Cumulative shares are more valuable to holders than non-cumulative ones because arrears are not lost.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to a missed dividend on non-cumulative preference shares?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is forfeited for that year, with no arrears carried forward.

items.title: Why issue preference shares, and how they are redeemed
items.core_explanation_md:
**Reasons to issue:** **no security** (no charge on assets) needed, **deposit regulations do not apply**, **flexible medium-term maturity**, and **dividends can be skipped** in a loss year (unlike **interest**). They suit **good-record firms near their debt limit**.

**Cost:** **dividend / issue price**; dividends are **not tax-deductible**, so there is **no interest tax shield**.

**Redemption** must **not reduce shareholder funds**: either **redeem out of a fresh issue of shares** or **transfer distributable profits to a Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR)**, usable **only for bonus shares**. **CRR transfer = nominal value redeemed - proceeds of fresh issue applied**.

**Securities premium** from a fresh issue may be used only for **specified purposes** (for example **bonus shares**, **preliminary expenses**, **issue costs**, **premium on redemption**).

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{CRR transfer} = \text{Nominal value redeemed} - \text{Fresh issue proceeds applied}

variables.name: Nominal value of the preference shares redeemed
Proceeds of a fresh issue used for the redemption

assumptions: Shares are fully paid
Redemption from profits is permitted
common_errors: Treating the transfer as a distribution to shareholders
Forgetting the fresh issue offset

items.expanded_explanation_md: The reserve keeps outsiders protected by leaving the same level of capital behind after redemption.

self_check.prompt_text: What may the Capital Redemption Reserve be used for?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Only to issue fully paid bonus shares.

items.title: Perpetual non-cumulative preference shares of banks
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks issue **perpetual non-cumulative preference shares (PNCPS)** as part of **Additional Tier 1 capital**.

**Principles:** **issued by the bank**, **fully paid**; **no maturity**, **no step-up**, **no incentive to redeem**; **dividends fully discretionary** and **not cumulative**; **no put option**; a **call only after a minimum period**, **with regulator consent**, and only if the capital is **replaced** or well above the minimum; **repayment needs regulator approval**; **ranks above equity** but **below depositors and creditors**; **loss-absorbing** through **conversion to common shares or write-down at a trigger**.

The **limits and percentages** in the courseware are **not taught** because they are revised.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These features make the instrument behave like permanent capital that can absorb a bank loss.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a bank cancel dividends on PNCPS without default?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The dividends are fully discretionary and non-cumulative, so cancellation is not a default.

items.title: Features of warrants
items.core_explanation_md:
A **warrant** gives the holder the **right, not the obligation**, to buy a **fixed number of equity shares** at a **fixed price** within a **set period**.

- Often **attached to debt** to **sweeten** the terms, or issued to **promoters and institutions** on a **preferential basis** to raise their stake if the firm does well.
- **No dividend or voting rights** until **converted into shares**.
- **Preferential issue:** part of the price is **paid up front**, **adjusted** against the final payment and **forfeited** if the warrant is **not exercised**.
- To protect **minority holders**, the **conversion price** in a preferential issue **cannot be below a floor** linked to **recent market prices** (periods not taught).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the holder can walk away, the upfront amount is the issuer protection against a non-exercise.

self_check.prompt_text: Do warrant holders receive dividends before exercise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, they have no dividend or voting rights until the warrant is converted into shares.

items.title: Convertible debentures: conversion ratio and conversion price
items.core_explanation_md:
A **convertible debenture** can be turned into **equity shares**, in **full (FCD)** or **part (PCD)**. Conversion **terms** (ratio, price, timing, premium) are **disclosed**.

**Conversion ratio (CR) = number of shares per debenture.**
**Conversion price = par value / CR.**
**Conversion value = CR x current share price.**
**Conversion premium = (conversion price - market price) / market price.**

Example pattern: a **Rs 100 debenture** convertible into **5 shares** has **CR 5** and **conversion price Rs 20**.

At issue the conversion price is usually **20 to 30 per cent above the market price**; ratio and price **stay fixed**, with a clause **protecting holders against dilution** from **bonus issues, splits and low-priced equity sales**.

assumptions: The ratio is fixed at issue
Anti-dilution adjustments are applied if needed
common_errors: Dividing the market price by the ratio
Confusing conversion price with the market price

items.expanded_explanation_md: The conversion premium measures how far the share price must rise before conversion pays.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the conversion price computed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The par value of the debenture divided by the conversion ratio.

items.title: Warrants versus convertible debentures
items.core_explanation_md:
Both give a **call option on equity**. Differences:

| Point | Warrant | Convertible debenture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Separability** | Can be **detached** from an attached debenture | Option **cannot be separated** |
| **Standalone issue** | **Yes** | No: it is a debt instrument |
| **Exercise** | **Cash payment**: **new capital** enters the firm | **Accounting transfer** only: **no new capital** |
| **Call provision** | Usually **cannot be cancelled** | Most carry an **issuer call** to **refund or force conversion** |
| **Life** | Usually **shorter** | Often **longer** |
| **Forfeiture** | Upfront payment **forfeited** if not exercised (preferential issue) | **None** for optionally convertible debentures |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Exercise of a warrant raises money; conversion of a debenture only swaps debt for equity.

self_check.prompt_text: Which instrument brings new capital into the company when the option is used?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A warrant, because the holder pays the exercise price in cash.

items.title: Valuation of a warrant: bounds and the Black-Scholes model
items.core_explanation_md:
A warrant is a **call option** on the issuer equity.

**Intrinsic value = max(S - E, 0)**. The **maximum** value of a warrant is the **stock price**; the **lower bound** is the **intrinsic value**. The price lies between.

**Premium over the minimum rises with:** **volatility**, **time to expiry**, **risk-free rate** and **stock price**; **it falls with the exercise price**.

**Black-Scholes:** **C = S x N(d1) - E x e^(-rt) x N(d2)**

**d1 = [ln(S/E) + (r + sigma^2 / 2) t] / (sigma x sqrt t)**; **d2 = d1 - sigma x sqrt t**.

**Steps:** 1) find **d1 and d2**; 2) read **N(d1) and N(d2)** from tables; 3) compute **E / e^(rt)**; 4) **substitute**.

**Limits:** assumes **no dividends** and **ignores dilution** from exercise.

formula_spec.latex_expression: C = S N(d_1) - E e^{-rt} N(d_2)
assumptions: No dividends are paid before expiry
Dilution from exercise is ignored
Volatility is constant
common_errors: Using the simple rate instead of the continuous rate
Using E instead of its present value in the second term

items.expanded_explanation_md: A larger volatility or longer life raises the value because the option has limited downside.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two limits of applying Black-Scholes to a warrant.
self_check.expected_takeaway: It ignores dividends and the dilution caused when warrants are exercised.

items.title: Valuing and costing convertible debentures
items.core_explanation_md:
A **partly convertible debenture** has **three parts**: **interest** through the life, **equity shares** on part conversion and **repayment of the non-convertible principal**.

**Value to the investor** = **PV of interest at the required return on debt** + **PV of the expected value of the shares received at the required return on equity** + **PV of principal instalments at the required return on debt**.

**Cost to the issuer:** use **after-tax interest** and find the rate that **equates the net subscription price to the discounted flows**.

**Optionally convertible:** valued like a **compulsorily convertible** one, but the market may pay a **premium for the option to decline conversion**; its value **can never be below** that of a similar compulsorily convertible debenture.

variables.name: Expected value of shares received at conversion

assumptions: Cash flows are certain in timing

common_errors: Discounting the share value at the debt rate
Ignoring the tax shield in the issuer cost

items.expanded_explanation_md: Each part is discounted at the rate that fits its risk: debt flows at the debt rate and shares at the equity rate.

self_check.prompt_text: At what rate is the expected value of shares received on conversion discounted?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At the investor required return on equity.

items.title: Why companies issue warrants and convertibles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Conventional explanations:** **cheap debt** and **selling equity later at a higher price**. The courseware says these are **not persuasive**.

**Modern finance explanations:**

- **Matching of cash flows:** the **low initial interest burden** suits a **developing, risky** firm; if it succeeds, holders **convert** and **dilution is welcome**.
- **Financial synergy:** when the issuer **risk is hard to assess**, a convertible is a **straight debenture plus a call option** whose values **move in opposite directions**: a **risky** firm has a **low debenture value and a high option value**, a **safe** firm the reverse, so the **required return is not very sensitive** to the risk estimate.
- **Agency costs:** **equity holders favour risk, bondholders safety**; convertible holders **share the upside**, so they worry less about **risk-taking** and **covenants can be lighter**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The two parts of a convertible hedge each other, which makes it easier to price an uncertain issuer.

self_check.prompt_text: How does a convertible reduce the conflict between bondholders and shareholders?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Convertible holders share the upside of risk-taking, so they care less about the company taking risk.

items.title: Foreign currency convertible bonds
items.core_explanation_md:
A **FCCB** is a bond in a **foreign currency** (often the **US dollar**) with **coupon and principal** plus an **option to convert into equity** at a **set conversion price**.

- Holders **convert only if the share price is above the conversion price**; otherwise they **redeem** at maturity.
- Often has an **issuer call** and a **holder put**.
- **Coupon is lower** than on a straight bond because of the option, so the **cost to the issuer is lower**.
- **Risks to the issuer:** **exchange rate** (a weaker rupee raises the servicing cost), **country, political and legal risks**, and **repayment at maturity** if holders do not convert.
- Typical **term about five years**.
- Holders carry **exchange rate and credit risk**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The cheap coupon can be wiped out if the rupee falls against the bond currency.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the FCCB coupon lower than on a plain bond?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Investors accept less because the conversion option has value.

items.title: Mezzanine financing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Mezzanine finance** is a **hybrid of debt and equity**: the **lender can convert the debt into equity if the borrower defaults**.

- Used for **specific projects or acquisitions**.
- **Higher returns** for the investor; often **unsecured**.
- Interest may be **partly fixed and partly variable**.
- Usually matures in **more than five years**, in line with the **existing debt**.
- In the issuer books it is carried as **debt**.
- It ranks **below senior debt**, so it is **costlier than senior debt** but **cheaper than equity**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: It fills the gap between senior loans and pure equity in the financing stack.

self_check.prompt_text: What right does a mezzanine lender have on default?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The right to convert the debt into equity.

items.title: Innovative hybrids
items.core_explanation_md:
**Innovative hybrids** combine a **bond or share** with a **derivative** (forward, swap or option).

| Hybrid | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Convertible bearer eurobond** | **Lower coupon** than comparable straight bonds |
| **Commodity-linked bond** | **Repayment tied to a commodity price** above a base level |
| **Dual-currency bond** | **Interest in one currency, principal in another**, to manage **exchange risk** |
| **Collared floating-rate note** | **Floating rate with a floor and cap**; the investor accepts the cap for a **higher rate** |
| **Rating-sensitive note** | **Spread rises if the issuer rating falls**, easing **bondholder-shareholder disputes** |

**Why they spread:** they **complete markets** and may offer **tax or regulatory benefits**. **Critics** call many a **supply-driven fad** pushed by bankers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A collar limits both the downside and the upside for the investor.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a collar on a floating-rate note do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It sets a minimum rate (floor) and a maximum rate (cap) on the coupon.

items.title: What a start-up is and the Start-up India initiative
items.core_explanation_md:
A **start-up** is a business that is **just getting started**: created by one or more owners to supply a good or service for which they see a market. It typically has **high costs and little income**, so it seeks **outside funding** (venture capital and other sources).

It is a company or project that seeks to **develop and validate a scalable business model**, with **high uncertainty and a high failure rate**; a **minority** become successful and influential.

**Start-up India** is run by the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**. It includes an **online hub** and a **recognition process**. The **Action Plan of January 2016** made recommendations in **three groups**: **financial assistance and incentives**, **industry-academia collaboration**, and **simplification and handholding**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Statistics on recognised firms and unicorns in the courseware are narrative and are not taught.

self_check.prompt_text: Which department runs Start-up India?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).

items.title: Benefits and support for start-ups
items.core_explanation_md:
Start-ups recognised under the plan can receive:

- **Tax incentives** and **government funding support**.
- **Priority and relaxed conditions in public procurement**.
- **Self-certification** of compliance with some **labour and environmental laws** and **relaxed inspection**.
- **Fast-track exit**: eligible start-ups can be **wound up in a shorter period** under the insolvency law.
- **Rebates on patent and trademark filing fees** and **faster patent examination**.
- **Incubators**: institutions giving **capital, laboratories, technology, networking, mentoring and advice**.

**Percentages, periods and amounts are not taught.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: The mix is meant to lower early-stage compliance cost and speed up a decision to close a failed venture.

self_check.prompt_text: What does an incubator provide to a young business?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Capital, technological and laboratory resources, networking, mentoring and advice.

items.title: Challenges faced by start-ups and state start-up policy
items.core_explanation_md:
**Main challenges:** **poor planning**, **unrealistic expectations**, **knowledge and skills gaps**, **time management**, **weak leadership**, **fierce competition and lack of demand**, **winning customer trust**, **hiring**, **partnership decisions**, **financial management**, **securing funding** and **cyber security**.

**State start-up policy:** a state policy gives **funding, mentorship and market access**, and **incentives to incubators and higher education institutions**, so that a **local ecosystem** develops. Most states and union territories have one.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Many failures come from weak planning and finance rather than from the idea itself.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two challenges that start-ups face.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example securing funding and fierce competition (any two from the list).

items.title: The pitch presentation
items.core_explanation_md:
A **pitch** is a **short slide presentation** that shows the business and gives investors **reasons to invest**. It became common in the **late 1990s dotcom boom**.

**It should be** **clear and concise**, stress the **most important points** rather than every detail, **answer the investor main questions**, be **flexible** to the type of venture and **address investor concerns**.

**Contents:** **problem statement**, **solution**, **business model**, **technology**, **business and commercial activity**, **competitive environment**, **team**, **predictions and significant events**, **present status and timelines**, **executive summary and call for action**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Investors back the team and the problem first, so these appear early in a pitch.

self_check.prompt_text: Name four items that a pitch should cover.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example the problem, the solution, the business model and the team.

| **Incubator grant challenges** | Fund and improve **incubators** |
| **Outreach programmes** | Reach **smaller cities and districts** |
| **Procurement support** | **Relax tender conditions**; a **marketplace section** for start-ups to sell to government |
| **Awards and rankings** | **Recognise start-ups** and **rank states** (access to markets, incubation, institutions, innovation, funding, capacity building, mentoring) |
| **Sector grand challenges** | **Solve problems in a sector**: health, water, energy, textiles, plastics, mining and others |
| **Women-focused programmes** | Training, platform and **funding links** for women entrepreneurs |
| **Innovation zones, research parks** | Local **civic problems** and **research capacity** |

items.title: Tax and regulatory reliefs for start-ups (purposes)
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes reliefs of these kinds:

- Relief from **tax on the issue of shares above fair value** for eligible start-ups.
- **ESOP taxation** with **deferral** for eligible start-ups, easing the **cash burden** on employees.
- A **deduction for a block of years** for eligible start-ups.
- **Capital gains relief** for individuals who **reinvest in start-up equity**.
- **Conditions** for **carrying forward losses**.
- **Relaxed deposit rules** for **convertible notes** taken by a start-up.

items.title: Principles of a seed fund scheme
items.core_explanation_md:
**Aim:** support **proof of concept, prototype development, product trials, market entry and commercialisation**, so the firm can later attract **angels, venture capital or bank loans**.

**Start-up eligibility (principles):** **recognised**, **young**, a **marketable technology-using idea**, and **not already heavily funded** by other schemes.

**Machinery:** **selected incubators** choose start-ups through a **selection committee**; an **expert committee** oversees the scheme.

**Controls:** funds go **only to start-ups** (not to build facilities), are paid **in instalments against milestones**, are held in a **dedicated account**, are **reported** against indicators, and **no fees** are charged to start-ups.

**Two uses:** **grants** for **validation** (prototype, proof of concept, trials); **investment** in **convertible debentures, debt or debt-linked securities** for **market entry or commercialisation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Milestone-linked instalments limit the loss if a venture fails early.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are seed funds paid in instalments against milestones?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It keeps funds tied to progress and limits the loss if the venture fails.

items.title: Fund of funds and credit guarantee
items.core_explanation_md:
**Fund of funds (FoF):** set up to **increase capital for start-ups**, **stimulate private investment** and **expand the ecosystem**.

- It does **not invest directly** in start-ups.
- It commits capital to **SEBI-registered alternative investment funds (AIFs), the daughter funds**, which then **invest in start-ups**.
- The **managing development bank** **selects and monitors** the daughter funds.

**Credit guarantee:** a **guarantee for the lender** that makes it **easier for early-stage entrepreneurs to borrow** by **reducing the collateral burden**.

**Sector programmes** (patents, renewable refinancing, biotechnology grants, defence technology, high-risk research) have **specific eligibility** that is **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Using AIFs spreads the investment decisions to professional managers.

self_check.prompt_text: How does a fund of funds reach start-ups?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Indirectly, by investing in alternative investment funds that invest in start-ups.

items.title: Equity round arithmetic: ownership, valuation and dilution
items.core_explanation_md:
Selling equity means **giving a share of ownership for capital**. Standard arithmetic:

- **Post-money value = pre-money value + investment.**
- **Investor stake = investment / post-money value.**
- **Price per share = pre-money value / shares before the round**; **new shares = investment / price per share.**
- **Founder stake after a round = stake before x (1 - stake sold).** Repeated rounds **multiply** the retention factors.
- **Runway (months) = cash / monthly net burn**, where **net burn = expenses - revenue**.

Debt avoids dilution but needs **interest and repayment** and sometimes **collateral**.

assumptions: All new shares are issued at the round price
No other securities are issued in the round
common_errors: Dividing by the pre-money value instead of post-money value
Adding the percentages of successive rounds instead of multiplying retention

items.expanded_explanation_md: A higher pre-money value lets founders give up less ownership for the same amount raised.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the investor stake in an equity round calculated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The investment divided by the post-money value.

items.title: Venture capital and why it exists
items.core_explanation_md:
**Venture capital (VC)** is a form of **private equity** supplied to **new enterprises and start-ups** that may **grow rapidly**. It brings **money and know-how**, and the investors expect a **high return**.

**Why it exists** (gaps in bank lending):

- Banks lend against **tangible collateral**; new businesses have **few assets**.
- The **risk is so high** that a lending rate high enough to compensate would be **prohibitive**.
- A VC takes a **share of the company** instead and so **shares the upside**.
- A VC adds **strategic guidance**, not only funds.

In India, **development financial institutions** supplied risk capital first; **foreign investors** later brought **rigorous due diligence, track-record tests, active post-investment involvement and a focus on timely exit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The investor accepts equity-style risk because a loan would price the risk out of reach.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do banks seldom finance a brand-new venture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The venture has little collateral and its risk is too high to price in an interest rate.
